#727. ‘In Starland’: How Ray Panthaki, in His Directing Debut, Cast Clarence Maclin in His First Lead Role and Made a Very Personal Film Built on Meritocracy

Bella Maclean ('Rivals') and Miss Benny ('Club Kid') also feature in the Tallinn-premiering, Killer Films-backed "non-dependent" movie. Shares Maclin: “There was something special about making this film."

Ray Panthaki (Boiling Point, Colette, Gangs of London) makes us think about modern culture in his feature directorial debut, In Starland. Clarence Maclin (Sing Sing) stars in his, unbelievably, first lead role. The cast also features Bella Maclean (Rivals) and Miss Benny (Club Kid), among others.

Maclin is Ernie, 50, who lives a quiet and unremarkable life – until he becomes involved with online content creators in their 20s. “Finding a place where he finally belongs, Ernie discovers a world of hedonistic pleasure and voyeurism in which every movement he makes begins to blur the boundaries between performance and reality,” reads a synopsis on the website of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia, where the film celebrates its world premiere on Thursday, Nov. 19. “As he searches for an identity lost in a mysterious past, fractures begin to appear between his newfound friends and the town of which he has been a part of for so long, and Ernie begins to wonder about the cost of his newfound notoriety.” Related Stories Movies European Lifetime Achievement Award for the Dardenne Brothers Music Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender Set to Headline Glastonbury 2027

Panthaki wrote the script with Jason Kavan and also produced the film with Daniel Khalili, Daisy Allsop and Victor Paul Wajnberg. Jaime Ackroyd is the cinematographer, with editing by Iain Kitching. Le Bateau Lavoir, Archface Films and Christine Vachon‘s Killer Films produced In Starland.

“I haven’t slept properly in years,” Panthaki shares. “But I made a film that I wanted to make with 100 percent creative control. I didn’t want to sell myself out to do the very thing I’m talking about in the movie – about numbers dictating life.”

When he wrote and directed the short film Life Sentence, Panthaki realized that he loved those behind-the-scenes roles. “That film was about something that was really personal to me,” Panthaki tells THR in Tallinn. “And when it came to getting made, I didn’t want anyone else to make it. I’ve lost someone close to me, so this was a story that I had to tell. It was a five-day shoot on a short film with a minuscule budget, and I realized when I stepped on set that this, in some ways, comes more naturally to me than acting. So I realized it was a massive calling.”

In Starland is also very close to Panthaki’s heart, comparing it to a child. “I realized that the first feature film, which is why it’s taken so many years, had to be something very personal, something that I wanted to say about the world,” he shares.

And he realized early on that his directorial feature debut came with bigger-picture goals. “I wanted to correct some wrongs that have happened to me as an actor in my career,” he tells THR. “I’ve found it frustrating sometimes that this industry is not a meritocracy. I’ve been offered roles where everyone on the film wants you, and then the head of the studio says, ‘Oh, actually, we want a bigger name. And so this was an opportunity for me to really get the right people for the right roles.”

In that context, Panthaki also calls the film “non-dependent because I don’t think independent gives the true story. “If a film that has got public funding is called ‘independent,’ then this has to have a different name, right? So I’ve been calling it non-dependent, which has been hard and frustrating at times. But the payoff for that was that I’m allowed to do things that other films can’t. For example, I was allowed to make this a meritocracy, and I’m so proud of that Clarence was the only actor out of the 11 lead actors whose previous work I had seen [before making In Starland]. When I watched Sing Sing, I was like, ‘This guy is captivating.’ There is something in his eyes that you just cannot deny.”

Maclin lauds Panthaki for his conviction and vision. “Ray sees the world in his own way, and you can feel that in this film,” the star tells THR. “He knows what he wants, but he’s also open to what you bring to it. He gives you room to be yourself, to try things, to find something you maybe didn’t even know was there. And that’s where the magic happens.”

In Starland premieres at a time when more of its cast members have broken out. “Miss Benny is, of course, in Club Kid,” notes Panthaki. “Then you got Bella, who is everywhere, and Ta’imua, this amazing Hawaiian actor, was in an Oscar-nominated short [Jane Austen’s Period Drama] playing a lead role. Everyone’s having their moment.”

While In Starland follows a group of young creators obsessed with views, likes and followers, “I didn’t want to know about the cast’s follower count,” the director recalls. “It was only about whether that person would earn the role in the room, and they did.”

And he needed actors happy to improvise. “That is how I like to do things,” the writer-director explains. “Once I have a script, I like to find truth and play around and naturalize things as much as possible. So I needed actors who were able to do that. I needed actors that I work very much on instinct, so I could turn up on a day and say, ‘This doesn’t feel right to me today. We’re going to do something completely different.’ That happened a number of times on set.”

That and the overall non-dependent nature of In Starland made the experience on set different. “There was something special about making this film,” Maclin shares. “We didn’t have all the things a big Hollywood production might have, but we had people who believed in what we were doing. And Ray, he wasn’t gonna compromise on what he wanted this film to be. You gotta respect that. When somebody believes in something that much, you wanna be part of it.”

In Starland leaves certain things open, unanswered or answerable in different ways. “I want people to have different opinions of what happens and instigate conversation,” Panthaki explains.

“What I love about In Starland is it ain’t trying to give you all the answers,” Maclin also emphasizes. “There’s some funny moments, there’s some painful moments, but there’s a whole lot of humanity in there. It makes you look at people a little differently, maybe think about things you hadn’t thought about before. And to me, that’s what storytelling is about.”

How did Killer Films end up boarding In Starland? “We asked Christine if she’d take a look and read the script and watch what we shot,” Panthaki says. “We had a conversation with her and over many conversations she just believed in the project. For me, that someone of that clout and and someone who has that amazing body of work believed in it is the biggest seal of approval. I’m so grateful to her and to Mason Plotts [, head of film at Killer Films].”

Audience will recognize 1980s music throughout In Starland. Given his own love for it, Panthaki says that he simply had to make one of his young characters be obsessed with music from that period. One of the key tunes in the film is the Tears for Fears hit “Everybody Wants to Rule the World.”

The director recalls reached out to the band himself. “I just wrote a letter, and I just told them why I’m doing this, what I’m trying to say about the world, and I don’t know if they ever read the letter or not,” Panthaki explains. “I actually wrote a number of letters during this process, and they came back and said, ‘Yeah, we’re willing to give the song to you for this amount of money.” I was never asking for it for free. I was asking for it for what we could afford within our means, and and they agreed to it.”

Asked about the film’s title, Panthaki tells THR: “I wanted something that felt poetic and really explained what the film was in a number of ways, and it just came to me. In Starland was a play on words because if you put those words together, it almost sounds like Instaland, so it has the Instagram element, and Ernie was in starland – but I don’t want to talk about a key twist there. I wanted to have a duality in the title, much like the lives of the people in the film.”

Could we see another feature directed by Panthaki? “Writing, directing and producing this film has been the hardest thing I’ve ever done in my life,” he shares. “Everything that has happened in this movie over the past seven years has been 10 times harder because we were doing it ourselves. So, will I do it again? I think yes. But I don’t know if I can do it again with so little time and money. I think I’ll need more infrastructure in place to be able to do it again.”

That said, Panthaki’s passion is coming through again. “I have ideas that are burning in me, and it has to be something I want to say about the world,” he tells THR. “It has to be something important that I can say, and something that I can do well. So I’ve got a couple of ideas that I’m working on. But for right now, get me back to acting!”

The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program.

The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad, commander, and Alan Bean, the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon, the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms.

The previous moon mission, Apollo 11, drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3. Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old.

Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions.

To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible.

The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13.

The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. #725. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#724. Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water

Earth may have created a substantial amount of its own water as the planet was forming, rather than relying entirely on comets, meteorites, or other objects to deliver it from space. New research published in Nature Geoscience suggests that chemical reactions between rocky pebbles and the hydrogen-rich atmosphere of the young Earth could have produced enormous quantities of water.

The discovery offers a new explanation for how our planet acquired one of the most important ingredients for life. It also raises the possibility that other rocky planets throughout the universe could generate water through similar processes, potentially making habitable worlds more common than previously thought.

Researchers at The University of New Mexico investigated this possibility by recreating some of the extreme conditions that existed during Earth's formation. The study was led by graduate student Susmita Garai, along with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson. Their experiments examined what happens when rocks containing iron react with hydrogen at extremely high temperatures.

"Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism," explained Sharp. "In order to evaluate the possibility of 'pebble' rain' being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai's efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earth's atmosphere."

A New Explanation for the Origin of Earth's Water

For decades, scientists have debated where Earth's water originally came from. One prominent theory suggests that much of it was transported to the developing planet by icy material originating in the colder, more distant regions of the early solar system.

According to this explanation, water-rich objects, including small icy pebbles, traveled inward and eventually contributed to Earth's water supply. However, researchers have struggled to fully explain how enough of this material could have reached our planet from such great distances. There are also unresolved questions about whether this delivery process accounts for Earth's chemical composition.

The new study investigates a different route by which water could have appeared. Instead of arriving already contained in ice or other materials, water may have been produced directly through reactions involving the rocky ingredients that built Earth and the gases surrounding it.

During the planet's earliest stages, countless small pieces of rock gradually came together to form a larger body. Scientists refer to this growth process as pebble accretion. As Earth gained mass, it could have accumulated a dense atmosphere containing large amounts of hydrogen, with temperatures and pressures far higher than those found on the planet today.

Under those conditions, rocky pebbles falling through the atmosphere could have triggered a remarkable chemical reaction. Hydrogen in the surrounding gas would react with iron oxide inside the silicate rocks, transforming the iron oxide into metallic iron while releasing water vapor.

Experiments Reveal Water Can Form in Minutes

To determine whether this process could actually occur, the researchers exposed samples of silicate rock to temperatures ranging from 1,200 to 1,400 degrees Celsius. They conducted experiments using flowing hydrogen gas and repeated the tests with helium to provide a comparison. Each experiment ran for between 15 minutes and three hours.

The results provided strong evidence that the proposed reaction works under these extreme conditions. When the rocks were heated in hydrogen, almost 80% of their iron oxide was transformed into metallic iron, with water vapor produced during the reaction.

In contrast, the researchers did not observe the same reaction when helium was used instead of hydrogen. This difference confirmed that hydrogen played a crucial role in generating the water.

The speed and scale of the reaction were especially striking. Although the scientists had expected some water to form, the results suggested that the process could have been far more productive than anticipated. When they extended their experimental findings to conditions on the early Earth, their calculations indicated that the mechanism might have generated hundreds of oceans' worth of water.

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans' worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have," said Sharp.

Earth's Fiery Beginnings May Have Helped Create Its Oceans

These findings suggest that the conditions of Earth's formation may have actively contributed to its water supply. Rather than being entirely dependent on water delivered from elsewhere in the solar system, the growing planet may have possessed the ingredients needed to manufacture water through its own chemical reactions.

The implications extend well beyond Earth. If rocky planets around other stars develop similarly hot, hydrogen-rich atmospheres during their formation, they might also produce substantial amounts of water as rocky material accumulates.

This possibility could have important consequences for understanding how common water is across the universe. A process that naturally occurs during the formation of Earth-sized planets would mean that obtaining water might not require the right icy objects to arrive from distant regions of a planetary system.

Could Other Earth-Like Planets Make Their Own Water?

The research also adds to growing interest in pebble accretion as an explanation for how planets form. Although the concept has gained attention relatively recently, it has already helped scientists address several longstanding questions about planetary development.

"The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It's only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation," Sharp said. "And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life."

There are still important uncertainties to resolve. While the experiments show that rocky material can generate water when exposed to hydrogen under conditions resembling those of the early Earth, they do not establish how much of our planet's present water supply was actually produced this way. Additional research will be needed to determine the contribution of this mechanism compared with water delivered by comets, meteorites, and other sources.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important process that may have shaped Earth billions of years ago. They also suggest that the ability to produce water could be built into the formation of rocky planets themselves, opening new possibilities for understanding where water, and perhaps life, might exist beyond our solar system.

Materials provided by University of New Mexico. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#723. Lee Chang-dong on the Mysteries and Meaning of ‘Possible Love’

The revered Korean auteur sits down with The Hollywood Reporter in Seoul to share the vision behind some of the most powerful moments in his Oscar-tipped new drama, which might just be the best film Netflix has ever made.

Lee Chang-dong believes in a god of cinema. But like any deity worthy of worship, the celebrated South Korean auteur’s higher power can’t simply be summoned when you feel you need it most.

“All through production, director Lee would talk to me and our assistant director about this movie god,” says Kim Ji-yong, the cinematographer on Lee’s acclaimed seventh feature and buzzy Oscar contender, Possible Love. “He said the god would only appear after we had tried everything — put all our ideas, all of our energy, into the film. Only then, the god might come down to show us something beautiful — something we never expected or imagined.” Related Stories Movies 'In Starland': How Ray Panthaki, in His Directing Debut, Cast Clarence Maclin in His First Lead Role and Made a Very Personal Film Built on Meritocracy Business Can Peter Rice Fix Netflix? New Content Boss Has a Daunting To-Do List

“He really believes this,” Kim adds. “He even told us stories about the handful of times in the past when the movie god appeared on his sets.”

The most recent visitation came nearly a decade ago, during the tail end of production on Lee’s beguiling 2018 dramatic thriller, Burning.

In the film’s violent, enigmatic climax, the young protagonist, Jong-su (Yoo Ah-in), meets his wealthy rival, Ben (chillingly inhabited by Steven Yeun), on a remote road outside Seoul. Jong-su approaches as if to chat, then plunges a knife into Ben’s stomach. He shoves the body into Ben’s silver Porsche, strips off his bloodied clothes, throws them inside and sets the car on fire. Within the complicated framing of the story, it’s unclear whether this episode actually happened or was imagined.

“That scene is shot as one long, continuous take during sunset, and they prepared for it very carefully,” Kim says, recounting Lee’s story. “And if you remember, just as [Jong-su] is walking back to his truck naked, with the burning car behind him, snow starts falling heavily.”

“This was the movie god, according to director Lee,” Kim adds. “They didn’t plan for it to snow in that moment; they couldn’t have. But it happened, and it’s so cinematic.”

Within the Korean film industry, it’s no exaggeration to say that Lee himself is regarded as something of a deity, or at least a national treasure.

Born in 1954 to an impoverished but educated family in the southern Korean city of Daegu, Lee began his working life as a high school teacher before establishing himself as a fiction writer. He won acclaim for stories delicately attuned to the agonies and ironies of Korea’s tumultuous postwar period, an era of brutal political repression and breakneck economic development. His characters tended to be sympathetic, disadvantaged outsiders — sensitive people placed in impossible predicaments by the wrenching forces of ideology and history.

In the early 1990s, filmmaker friends recruited him to write screenplays, and in 1997 he made his directorial debut with Green Fish, a social critique disguised as a noirish crime movie. The film featured the first performance from Song Kang-ho, who would later become a national treasure in his own right through films like Park Chan-wook’s Joint Security Area and Bong Joon Ho’s Memories of Murder and Parasite.

Earlier this year, Squid Game creator Hwang Dong-hyuk told me that witnessing his favorite novelist — Lee — suddenly become a filmmaker was the moment that made him want to pursue a life in cinema himself.

“I idolized him, and his career pivot kind of gave me courage to go for it,” Hwang said. “And then when I actually watched [Green Fish], it was stunning — like every film he has done since.”

Five films followed before Possible Love, each an emotionally searing and intellectually electrifying portrait of people pushed to society’s margins. With Peppermint Candy (1999), Lee issued a devastating state-of-the-nation statement by telling a ruined man’s life in reverse. Moving backward through two decades of political repression, state violence and economic upheaval, the film gradually reveals how an innocent, hopeful young man became both an instrument and a casualty of his country’s corruption. In Oasis (2002), he portrayed an extraordinary romance between a damaged ex-convict and a woman with severe cerebral palsy, reveling in the desires and imaginative freedom that the world around them refuses to acknowledge. The film earned Lee the Venice Film Festival’s best directing prize.

He returned five years later with Secret Sunshine (2007), which follows a bereaved mother through a crisis so harrowing that even the promise of faith and forgiveness becomes a source of existential torment. Secret Sunshine‘s Jeon Do-yeon won the Cannes Film Festival’s best actress award for her powerful performance, a first for a Korean star.

Then came Poetry (2010), which continued Lee’s fusion of generous, humanist drama with challenging philosophical inquiry, following an elderly woman who takes up writing poetry as she confronts the onset of Alzheimer’s and her grandson’s involvement in a horrific crime — her search for beauty becoming inseparable from the obligation to face a truth she would rather not see. Lee won Cannes’ best screenplay prize for the film.

And Burning (2018), finally, transformed a short story by Haruki Murakami into a mesmerizing mystery of class resentment, thwarted desire and the existential angst of Korea’s contemporary youth. It became the first South Korean film shortlisted for the foreign-language Oscar — an embarrassingly late milestone, given how much indelible cinema the country had already produced. But the Academy quickly made up for lost time at the 2020 ceremony, when Parasite, directed by Lee’s friend Bong Joon Ho, won four Oscars, including best picture.

Lee’s legendary status at home also stems from the fact that his contribution to Korean cinema has gone well beyond his own filmmaking. In the 1990s, he became a leading campaigner for enforcement of the country’s screen quota, which required theaters to show domestic movies for a minimum number of days each year. By protecting local filmmakers’ access to audiences from Hollywood dominance, the policy created space for ambitious Korean cinema to flourish throughout the 2000s — a driving force behind the broader Korean cultural wave still unfolding today. From 2003 to 2004, Lee even served as South Korea’s minister of culture and tourism.

Over the summer, I flew to Seoul to meet the mercurial auteur Na Hong-jin at his office on the city’s east side. A favorite of both action fans and art-house aficionados, Na studied under Lee as a graduate student at the prestigious Korea National University of Arts and later became an international cult sensation with a string of singularly twisted genre movies: the serial killer thriller The Chaser (2008), brutal crime flick The Yellow Sea (2010) and the supernatural freakout The Wailing (2016).

The occasion for our chat was the U.S. release of his divisive but wildly entertaining sci-fi action movie Hope. At the time, both his film and Lee’s Possible Love were viewed as leading contenders to represent South Korea in the international Oscar race. (Possible Love was ultimately selected and is now considered a frontrunner in the category.)

In what I thought would be a light, throwaway question, I asked how it felt to be competing with his former teacher. Na, who has a rather intense, skeptical bearing even when he’s feeling friendly, now grew more serious, and perhaps more skeptical of his interlocutor.

“As a filmmaker, Lee Chang-dong is basically a god to me,” he said, raising his voice a little and staring at me implacably. “I don’t compete with god, do you?”

Laughing at my startled reaction, he then softened his tone. “For those of us who came of age in the generations after him, Lee Chang-dong represents an older, in some ways better, era. His movies are difficult, but there’s a tolerance and understanding to his work that I find almost healing. I don’t know if this country still produces artists with that kind of depth.”

Lee’s movie god never appeared on the set of Possible Love — but the production was not without its moments of magic.

The film, which is currently streaming on Netflix globally, reunites Lee with Sul Kyung-gu, the unforgettable male lead of Peppermint Candy and Oasis, and Jeon of Secret Sunshine. Together, thanks in no small part to their performances in Lee’s films, they are now regarded as screen royalty in Korea, having won seven Grand Bell Awards between them, their country’s equivalent to the Oscars.

Sul plays Ho-seok, an autoworker left unemployed and profoundly damaged after a strike at his factory was violently suppressed by the state; Jeon is his loving, resourceful wife, Mi-ok, who works in a mask factory to keep their family afloat.

The drama begins to turn when their lives become unexpectedly entangled with those of an attractive couple from the opposite end of the class divide. Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, playing another rich wife as she famously did in Parasite) is an aspiring documentary filmmaker working on a project about workers’ rights in Korea, who becomes drawn to Ho-seok’s story. Her husband, Sang-woo (Hope’s Zo In-sung), is a dashing tycoon who seems happy to support her pursuits. The budding friendship among the foursome is warm, awkward and increasingly fraught, with Ye-ji’s attempts at empathy growing difficult to disentangle from her eagerness to make art from the other couple’s struggles.

The film culminates with a group trip to the coast. Hoping to convince Ho-seok to finally sit for a lengthy interview, Ye-ji invites the other couple to her husband’s luxurious seaside family home for a weekend away. (Production designer Jang Min-woo and his team built the house from scratch to Lee’s specifications.) Dinner on the first night becomes a messy drinking session. At dawn, Ho-seok staggers out toward the sea, and Mi-ok, curious about this exit, surreptitiously follows. The camera tracks them into a wind-tossed forest, where Ho-seok’s suppressed rage fully erupts into a PTSD-driven breakdown: Screaming, he thrashes his body against the trees and branches around him, as his wife secretly watches in silence.

As Mi-ok retreats in distress, she encounters Ye-ji in a clearing, attempting to film this painful private moment. The two women stare at each other from opposite edges of the frame as the wind howls and the trees sway behind them. This tableau, which captures so much of the story’s complex meta-fictional pathos, later became one of Possible Love‘s key marketing images.

Originally, in Lee’s script, the sequence was supposed to take place on a calm, clear morning, says Kim, the cinematographer.

“But on the day of our tech scout to the coast, it was a really windy day, and director Lee and I both thought it looked great,” he recalls.

One of his country’s most in-demand DPs, Kim is perhaps best known internationally for the baroque, highly stylized camerawork he employed on Park Chan-wook’s romantic thriller, Decision to Leave (2022). He also shot the hit second and third seasons of Squid Game. For Possible Love, Kim set aside his impressionistic approach and strove instead for the most naturalistic look he could achieve, shooting nearly the entire film with a handheld camera he carried himself and relying on natural light as much as possible.

“Director Lee agreed it would add a nice layer if we could shoot it in a heavy wind,” Kim recalls. “And since we would be filming at the house for a month, I convinced him we could get all prepped, but then wait to see if we got lucky with a windy day or two.”

He adds: “And in my head, I thought, ‘Okay, this is where we’ll meet the movie god, right?'”

“But then, that whole month: no wind. Not even a strong breeze.”

Although Lee is famous for the seriousness and solemnity with which he approaches his work, he is also widely admired in the Korean production world for the collaborative atmosphere on his sets.

Many leading auteurs readily discuss matters of craft but resist interpreting their work, preferring to leave its meaning to the audience. Lee believes it’s vital that his collaborators understand the ideas and nuances each scene is intended to convey. His cinema may ask philosophical questions that are ultimately irresolvable, but he is resolutely clear and intentional about how his choices put those questions into play.

“If someone asks him something about a scene, no matter who it is on the crew — maybe it’s like an assistant set dresser — he will stop and thoroughly explain the scene, his intentions, and how it fits into the whole movie,” Kim says. “I’ve worked on a lot of films, but I had never seen a director who is so patient and generous with his thoughts like that.”

So, when the winds never arrived for Possible Love‘s poignant sunrise moment, Lee’s team resolved to “create a crew god” for him instead.

“More than 100 people — the assistants, some of the cast, and every member of the crew except for three or four of us huddled around the monitor with director Lee — went into the forest and tied ropes to the trees and pulled like crazy so that the whole forest would sway like in a strong wind,” Kim recalls.

He adds: “It wasn’t anyone’s job, but we all did it, because we knew how much that scene meant to him — because he had told every one of us.”

Possible Love premiered at Venice in September, winning the festival’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. It later screened at the Toronto and New York film festivals, earning rave reviews at every stop. It currently has the highest Rotten Tomatoes score — 97 percent fresh from 112 reviews — of any major global release this year.

Possible Love was fully financed and produced by Netflix, and if the project seems a somewhat out-of-character choice for both Lee and the streamer (as more than a few critics have noted), it is also true that the film is the most critically acclaimed adult drama that the company has ever made — holding higher average review scores than any of the other entries on Netflix’s conspicuously short list of potential enduring classics (The Irishman, Marriage Story, The Power of the Dog, All Quiet on the Western Front and Frankenstein all rank slightly lower, for example, while other lasting favorites, such as Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma, were acquired but not produced by the streamer).

It is also the best-supported awards contender of Lee’s long but still-too-overlooked career. Netflix is mounting a multi-front Oscar campaign extending beyond the international category to best picture, best director, best original screenplay and the acting categories, with a particularly ambitious push for Jeon.

Netflix had quietly been courting Lee since the company launched operations in South Korea a decade ago.

“One of the top three rumors that’s always floating around the Korean film industry is that Lee Chang-dong has finished a new script,” says Minyoung Kim, Netflix’s top content executive in the Asia-Pacific region, who built the streamer’s formidable Korean operations from the ground up.

In recent years, Lee’s output has grown sporadic, with eight-year breaks between each of his last three features.

“The reason his films take so long is that he deeply, almost painfully, thinks about why a story needs to be told,” Kim explains. “Many directors are happy when they’ve found an entertaining idea that works, or a great piece of IP to adapt; with director Lee, it all starts with an observation about reality, or a question he can’t resolve about life.”

She says she’s aware of numerous potential projects — all of which sounded, to her creative exec ear, like compelling, ready-to-go premises — that Lee shelved because their themes didn’t feel urgent enough.

“So, every time we heard those rumors about a new script over the years, we checked in — just to be like, ‘We’re here; we’d love to work with you!'”

“You could even say we were a little clingy,” Kim adds, laughing.

Netflix’s opportunity to partner with Lee came after the auteur struggled to secure the relatively modest budget he was seeking for Possible Love — reportedly around 8 billion won, or roughly $6 million — after the key cast agreed to fee reductions to help him get the project made. South Korea’s prolonged post-pandemic box-office slump has left its major studios increasingly cautious about backing serious dramas, even with filmmakers and casts of this stature. Kim believes Lee would eventually have found a local financier, but the studios’ hesitancy gave Netflix its opening.

Netflix agreed to a larger, undisclosed budget and put its production resources behind the film. The commitment extended to a limited international theatrical release and substantial awards-season support, while leaving all creative decisions — including final cut — in Lee’s hands.

“On a lot of our shows, we try to understand the director’s vision, and become their thought partner. We debate and discuss, and try to make suggestions on what we believe will make the film stronger,” Netflix’s Kim explains. Describing Lee as a maestro, she says, “he didn’t need our opinions.”

She adds: “We just tried to understand his vision as fully as we could, so we could support him at every step of the way.”

The Hollywood Reporter recently spoke with Lee in Seoul about the creation of Possible Love and the ideas behind several pivotal scenes. The conversation includes spoilers.

From what I understand, Possible Love began more than a decade ago as a project about the workers involved in Korea’s real-life SsangYong Motor strike, which resembles the episode depicted in the film. You wrote a script and went into pre-production, then shelved it. What concerned you about that earlier version?

It’s true that the project began for me with the 2009 SsangYong Motor incident, but when I speak about the origins of the story today, I try not to mention the company or the specific year, because I don’t want too much emphasis placed on that particular incident. There have been many similar cases in the Korean labor movement, and I’d like the film to be viewed in that broader context. But yes, about 10 years ago, that case is what got me started. I did a lot of research, wrote a screenplay and went into preproduction. And then I shelved it — for two reasons.

First, I was constantly asking myself: What meaning does it have for me to turn this episode into a dramatic feature? What does it mean to me personally? What will it mean to the audience? And what meaning will it hold as a film in itself? I just couldn’t find answers I had real conviction in. There was already a documentary about the strike and the lives of the workers involved, and I felt it was a very honest and thorough piece of work. [Lee is referring to Seo Seh-chin’s 2009 documentary Before the Full Moon.] Ultimately, I didn’t see how I could add to what the documentary had already achieved simply by turning it into a dramatic feature.

The second factor was connected to feelings and beliefs I have long held as a creator. I was writing fiction back in the 1970s and 1980s, often about Korean society and the issues within it. Naturally, I wrote about my times, and because of what our country was going through, that meant writing about people who were suffering — people living under our authoritarian military government, factory workers facing hardship, students participating in the democracy movement and those hurting because of our divided nation.

And I always ended up asking myself, “Am I worthy of telling this story? Does it hold meaning for me to be the one saying this?” I asked these questions because my life and my situation were often very different from those of the people I was portraying. I wasn’t suffering as badly as they were. So what right did I have?

As I worked on the early versions of Possible Love, all these questions came back to me, and I couldn’t find conviction in any approach. So I shelved it.

Then, as the years passed, the issue of labor itself began to go through big changes. At the time of the strike, the focus was on the direct pain the laid-off workers were suffering as we entered a more global, capital-driven system — the suffering of those betrayed and abandoned. Now, that pain is becoming universal. The issue today is that labor itself is on the verge of disappearing. There is no longer as clear a line between the working class and the nonworking class, because we are beginning to see the disappearance of labor itself, and all the definitions of self that come with it. These shifts got me interested again, but I was still finding it difficult to move forward.

It was only when my co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, suggested placing a documentary filmmaker within the story that I began to see a path with some legitimacy. Now it was also my story, as the creator and teller of other people’s stories. It allowed me to question my own position: What are my attitudes? What’s built into the gaze I direct toward these people? And what should my ethics be?

That must have been such an exciting discovery — or simply a relief. With Ye-ji as your avatar, you seem able to express your best intentions as a storyteller while voicing your bitterly ironic self-doubts and unresolved questions about such storytelling. As a viewer, it feels like an ongoing, self-aware conversation with you.

You could also say that I gave myself an alibi. But this approach really did free me to tell their story without those earlier questions constantly tugging at my heart. It put me a little more at ease about telling the story of this laid-off worker and his family.

Strictly speaking, is Ye-ji my complete embodiment, my true avatar? Of course not. She and I are very different. But from a larger perspective, you could say that Ye-ji really does embody my best intentions and represents exactly who I am within the structure of this story. I felt this very keenly all over again at the world premiere in Venice. There I was in a very expensive rented tuxedo, walking a red carpet to present the story of a laid-off worker’s pain. I suppose some would say that is simply the nature of things, because filmmaking is married to capital.

Throughout the film, there are moments where characters seem to give direct voice to your self-conscious misgivings, as we’ve been discussing. Other questions are suggested by the plot, but aren’t stated quite so explicitly. One is related to the issue you just mentioned: Does art carry any real power to critique or change the capitalist system, or is the aesthetic itself just another part of the system’s healthy functioning? You certainly seem to be nudging us in the direction of the latter. Ye-ji, the film’s well-intentioned artist, after all, is married to and supported by a capitalist tycoon. The documentary she is making seems entirely genuine — but the fact remains that her real-life husband is executing a private equity deal to sell off the factory at the heart of her story the entire time. By extension, this feels not dissimilar to the fact that increasingly large swaths of the global movie business are owned by some of the very same tech giants and oligarchs that are driving the technological changes that will potentially bring about the elimination of labor you mentioned earlier.

This question goes to the very essence of the film industry, and art-making in general — and who in this world could give a clear answer to that, right? That said, I have never felt free of this question since the very beginning of my work as a filmmaker. It’s always there.

One answer, for me at least, is that I believe films must never turn a blind eye to the real world and the people living within it. By “turn a blind eye,” I mean that the lives you portray in your film should never be consumed simply as material or content for making your movie.

Of course, we’re talking about a very fine line. When you are dealing with people in pain — people suffering from the many paradoxes of life — you must ask yourself: Am I only consuming or exploiting their story, or am I really trying to start a conversation with the audience in a meaningful and creative way? That’s a very difficult question to answer with full conviction.

As a rule of thumb, I believe that the simpler the objective of your story becomes, the further you have probably drifted from reality. I believe that a film exists to ask questions of the audience. If your audience leaves the theater having only experienced catharsis — entertainment or pleasure — then you have probably treated your subject as little more than an exercise in consumption.

Let’s talk about the film’s dual climaxes at the vacation home. How should we interpret Mi-ok’s actions on the beach? I read them as both an attempt to experience the freedom Sang-woo so effortlessly enjoys and a way to reclaim some power over him.

Meanwhile, Ho-seok is finally sitting for Ye-ji’s camera. I felt this terrible apprehension — I didn’t want him to give her this, as though she might artistically prey on him in the way you just described. But later I realized he’s doing this for his own reasons: He needs to open up and begin healing for his wife and son. Later, back home, he can finally use the little marble drinking station he built, and he seems a touch healed. So, both moments ultimately felt heroic to me. Am I on the right track?

You’re right that Mi-ok’s actions on the beach are something she chooses for herself in the hope of reclaiming her freedom. But it would be wrong to say she’s only emulating what Sang-woo said he felt as a child. Of course, his story gave her a hint, or planted the seed, but what she’s actually trying to do is a little different.

I believe what Mi-ok wanted in that moment was to face Sang-woo with nothing between them, not even the clothes on their bodies — simply one human facing another. She realizes that everything she and Ho-seok have endured — all the setbacks, all the pain, all the difficulties — has had everything to do with the distorting power of capital, and nothing to do with their own efforts and worth. And she realizes that this power is wielded by people like Sang-woo.

So she wanted to face the person at the heart of that force with nothing between them, and these are the actions she is able to improvise in that moment. In a way, she also wanted to test the happiness of this other couple a little — to throw a pebble at the glass castle of these people who enjoy all the benefits of such power. She wants to face him as just another naked human, but she also wants to provoke him a little.

As for Ho-seok’s sequence, he decides to sit for Ye-ji’s camera even though he is fully aware that his emotions are going to be used to fulfill her hidden desires. But he also knows he needs to somehow bring it all out of himself — all his deep-rooted rage and sadness. At this point, he knows it can only heal him a little. I also believe Mi-ok knew this from the beginning, and this is why she agreed to her family being part of the documentary in the first place. She wanted Ho-seok to take part in the interview so that he might be healed in some way.

Then, after all is said and done, when they’re sitting together at that marble platform at the very end, there’s a sense that they’ve learned something through all of this.

That marble platform had been a symbol of Ho-seok’s despair and failure. It’s a place charged with his very Korean sentiments — his sense of responsibility for his family and for the co-workers he tried to treat as brothers. It’s symbolic of his typical Korean masculinity, all of which has been brutally betrayed and taken away from him.

But now, at the end, he is able to sit in that place again — next to his wife, who has always been there for him — and they look up at the moon and share a peaceful moment together again. The moon, you know, transcends everything — class, capital, even time. Anybody can look up at the moon.

That’s so beautiful. What does the title mean to you? We’re familiar with the notion of an impossible love — a great romance thwarted by circumstance. Here, you seem to give us a “possible” great love story while also showing what it really takes — the loyalty, strength, sacrifice, wisdom and generosity. Perhaps the film is also saying that even amid the loss of meaningful work and the identity that comes with it, dignity can be found in the work of loving one another? Or could the title refer to love between the artist and her subjects — like the budding friendship between Ye-ji and Mi-ok, which seems genuine despite their class differences? Or is it even broader: the love a more successful labor movement in today’s world would require?

Most simply, I wanted even the title of the film to be a question, and I thought Possible Love could do that. Most of the great love stories we remember are about whether the characters can overcome everything and finally end up together — whether their love comes to fruition. So Possible Love is a sort of paradox. I wanted the audience to ask all the questions you’re asking: What does a possible love mean, and what kind of love is really possible?

I was told by various people that the title was too difficult or confusing. But I think as you grow more familiar with it, it begins to feel just right.

You can say the film is about labor and class, and also the philosophy and ethics of filmmaking. But what it’s really about is human relationships. We live in a time when those relationships are deteriorating and we’re being separated. The nature of human connection is fundamentally changing. There is exploitation and disconnection, and sometimes we intentionally cut people out of our lives.

But I believe human relationships ultimately boil down to a question of love. The only path to healing those relationships is love. It doesn’t matter what kind of relationship it is — within a couple, between an artist and their subject or with the people you meet in everyday life. What is your fundamental attitude toward them? With the title, I wanted to ask: How do we answer the question of love? And what questions should we be asking ourselves about love?

The second time I watched the film, I noticed more ways in which your fictional drama borrows the formal elements of a documentary. We get classic talking-head sequences by watching Ye-ji shoot her film, and your flashbacks start to feel like documentary reconstructions. I even began to reconsider the rainbow motif: Mi-ok tells that poetic anecdote about her mother’s angry reaction to her picking up a work hose as a child, and later we see her son playing with a servant, spraying water and making a rainbow. This feels like a connection a documentary director might discover in the editing room and use as a visual metaphor to tie together the film’s themes. Am I projecting, or were you deliberately closing the gap between your work and Ye-ji’s via the film’s formal construction?

No, you’re correct. Near the start of the film, after we introduce Ye-ji as a documentary filmmaker, the cinematographer and I were very careful to make it clear whether you were looking through her camera or ours. But as the film goes on, we gradually blur that distinction. If you watch the film again, you might notice shots where you really can’t tell who is supposed to be behind the camera — me or Ye-ji.

But I didn’t only want to emulate a documentary’s structure. I wanted to be intimately connected with the content, too. Through my dramatic feature, I wanted to communicate the pain and suffering of these laid-off workers, which is exactly what Ye-ji wanted to capture. In that sense, I would say there is no demarcation between my intentions and hers.

The clearest example is the therapy session just before they go to the vacation home. We see interviews with four people who are either laid-off workers or their family members. They give their testimony, and it’s done in a very documentary style.

Now, that’s not something you would usually see in a dramatic feature. From a purely filmmaking perspective, the sequence is too long and feels quite out of place. If I had cut it, not only would the pacing have been better, but the story would have been more emotionally effective, because we could have brought the characters to the vacation home sooner, with more momentum. However, I thought the sequence was essential because, above all else, I needed my film to also be loyal to Ye-ji’s intentions. So I felt the documentary style had to be integrated into my film.

It’s incredible how artfully you pulled all of that off. Changing gears a bit, Korea’s great auteurs seem to have converged lately on the same essential question: what capitalism is doing to society and individual dignity. In the global film-buff hive mind, you, Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon Ho pretty much represent the trifecta of Korean masters. Parasite, No Other Choice and Possible Love share many of the same themes and big-picture concerns, expressed in your very different cinematic idioms. What do you make of this convergence? Is it simply a matter of the shared history and political tradition from which you emerged, even though you belong to slightly different generations?

This is a question I got quite often in Venice, usually posed in a way that suggested most filmmakers in other countries had moved past this. Why is Korea still making films about class conflict? I gave a pretty general answer that I think is probably true: Because Korea experienced such extreme economic development in such a short period, it touched every aspect of society, and it’s only natural that we continue to suffer from the aftereffects. And the filmmakers that you mentioned, we all experienced those extreme changes when we were sensitive young men. So, I suspect it’s as simple as that.

But while we deal with the same issues, I think what’s most different is our attitude toward cinema, or how we think of our films as we’re creating them. I’m probably quite different from both of them. I might be kind of an oddball compared to most filmmakers.

Many filmmakers love cinema for its own sake, and you can feel that love of moviemaking in their work — and it can be a wonderful thing. But I can only speak for myself. For me, making films is not the most important thing. I don’t know if this will come across the way I intend, but the reality and the ideas I’m trying to portray are more important to me than the film itself. I think that attitude is apparent in my films. That is why, compared to other filmmakers, my films are not entertaining. They’re difficult.

My last question isn’t my own. I recently interviewed Na Hong-jin in Seoul about Hope. He holds you in very high esteem, so when I mentioned I’d be speaking with you, I asked if he had a question for you. This was his question: Outside of your work as a novelist and filmmaker, what kind of human being do you think you are?

I would say that I am a very timid person, and because of that, I tend to spend too much time thinking about how I should live — and it makes me very, very tired. (Laughs)

SpaceX had hoped for a historic double-catch landing for the Starship Flight 15 booster and Ship. The booster didn't make it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that."

SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster.

The giant Starship rocket, a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history.

The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned. Instead of returning to its launch tower to be caught mid-air by the tower's metal "chopstick" arms, however, the rocket veered offshore and detonated its flight termination system. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that a guidance issue appeared to be the cause.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

"We were initially 'go' for a catch," Huot said during live commentary on Friday, about seven hours into the mission. "But in the later stages of the coast, the booster aborted itself for a GNC issue that it detected, and that put it into its contingency landing offshore." Super Heavy exploded a few feet above the waves of the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

GNC is short for Guidance and Navigation Control, a criticial system used by rockets to control their flight and ensure they remain on their planned course. Such a system is vital for any landing attempt by a Starship Super Heavy or Ship upper stage to ensure the vehicle returns to its landing site safely and doesn't veer off course to damage SpaceX's Starbase or surrounding populated areas.

In an update during SpaceX's Flight 15 coverage on Saturday, however, Huot said that Super Heavy's GNC system actually performed well.

"I did a disservice to our booster GNC guys last night," Huot said. "It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back. GNC triggered that abort; it was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, [it] detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location."

SpaceX is "still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that," he added on Saturday.

You can follow our Starship Flight 15 live updates for the latest on the mission.

Super Heavy is powered by a cluster of 33 Raptor rocket engines that fire simultaneously during liftoff to send the 41-story Starship megarocket into orbit. During Friday's launch, all 33 engines fired as planned for the ascent, Huot said.

One engine did drop out after stage separation, when Super Heavy dropped away from Ship and flipped over for a "boostback" burn to begin its trip back to Earth, Huot said on Friday.

"We had 32 out of the 33 booster engines lit for boostback, which started sending it back here to the launch site," he added.

That firing was followed by the booster's landing burn. In SpaceX's launch video, Super Heavy can be seen activating 13 of its Raptor engines as planned, followed by the abort and the booster steering itself to a contingency landing zone in Gulf waters.

"It did that hover, cut the engines off, the FTS — the flight termination system — triggered, and it splashed down in the water," Huot said on Friday. (The FTS is designed to destroy a booster in the event of an emergency.)

As its name suggests, Starship Flight 15 is SpaceX's 15th test flight of the giant rocket, but it will be the first to attempt to catch a Ship upper stage with the chopsticks. SpaceX has successfully caught Super Heavy boosters on three test flights to date.

Flight 15's Ship vehicle is in good health and will orbit Earth a total of 14 times before landing back at its launch pad in Starbase at around 4:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT) today, if all goes well.

"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground-tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said in Friday's mission update. (Flight 15 hauled 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, and a few of those spacecraft carried cameras for heat-shield inspection.)

SpaceX designed Starship to be fully reusable, with the company banking on that reusability to make it an affordable heavy-lift booster capable of a wide range of missions to low Earth orbit, the moon and eventually Mars.

NASA has picked Starship as one of two commercial landers to carry Artemis astronauts to the moon in 2028, and SpaceX sees the rocket as vital to building out a 100,000 constellation of Starlink V3 internet satellites, as well as a new AI data center network in orbit called Starmind.

But first, SpaceX has to successfully land a Starship upper stage from orbit. That's the next step for Flight 15.

Huot said that flight controllers will make one last check at the 20-hour mark in the mission to decide whether to proceed with the landing at Starbase or make an "early return" splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.

That final check is expected by about 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT). Space.com's Starship Flight 15 landing livestream will begin at that time, and will be carried on our live updates page, Space.com homepage and our VideoFromSpace YouTube page.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:50 a.m. ET on Nov. 14 with the latest information from SpaceX's Dan Huot, who clarified that the booster tower-catch abort was not caused by a GNC issue.

#721. Disney and AWS Team Up to Create AI-Powered ‘Star Wars’ Robots

The new creations, the Anzellans, will react to guests and each other in real-time, showcasing how AI could transform the theme park experience.

The Walt Disney Co. has hosted audio-animatronics at its theme parks going back to the opening of Walt Disney’s Enchanted Tiki Room in 1963. The decades since have seen presidents, beloved film characters and even Walt Disney himself turned into the audio-animatronics, relying on robots paired with scripted moments to complete the illusion for visitors.

But Disney and Amazon on Wednesday are pulling back the curtain on what Disney’s Imagineers think may be the next big thing in audio-animatronic technology: Robots with distinct personalities that can react to each other, and to visitors, powered by AI.

The audio-animatronic robots in question are The Anzellans: Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a, an alien species from the Star Wars galaxy that featured in the 2026 film The Mandalorian and Grogu that will make their public debut at Amazon re:Invent in Las vegas later this month. They were designed by Disney’s Imagineers, though they are powered by AWS.

“The work that we’re doing with Amazon dates back over a decade,” says Kyle Laughlin, senior VP, Walt Disney Imagineering R&D and Technology and Engineering, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “We’ve continued to work together in many different forums, everything from Disney+ to supporting Imagineering and the work that we do every day, and these three Anzellans from the Star Wars universe, originally in Solo, but most recently in Mandalorian and Grogu, are these incredible droidsmiths that we wanted to bring to life.”

The three robots each have cameras an microphones, with the AWS tech helping them determine what actions they take and alien phrases they should speak.

Samira Panah Bakhtiar, GM of Telco, Media & Entertainment, Games, Advertising and Sports for AWS, notes that the script and movements were all created by Imagineers, and the aliens don’t deviate from the movements and words written by the team, even if they use AI to help guide their actions.

“One of the things I’m most proud of at Amazon is how we obsess over making our customers successful and working backwards from their needs, and in this case, in this specific project, a group of AWS team members leveraged our coding tool called Kiro to be able to help take a lot of the ideas that the Imagineering team had and be able to help rapidly get it into a place where we could execute,” Bakhtiar says.

“I think that one of the unique things here is that each character is aware of three things happening at once,” she adds. “They’re aware of the guests in front of them, they’re aware of what’s happening in the workshop, and then they’re also perfectly aware of what the other characters are doing within the scene. And keeping track of all three of those at once really gives that experience that that they’re alive, and their reflexes and their judgments like all become part of that really unique guest experience.”

“I think what our guests you know are overwhelmingly saying all the time is that they want those character interactions that feel authentic and genuine, and as you mentioned, our audio animatronics today are very scripted in terms of how that interaction happens,” Laughlin adds. “When we launch with the Anzellans at [Amazon] re:Invent, it’ll be really the first time in which we will personalize that experience based on who that guest is.”

For now, the Anzellans will only be available to view at re:Invent, though it doesn’t take much to imagine that they will end up in the Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge worlds in California and Orlando eventually.

Still, the new robots demonstrate how Disney may ultimately use AI to improve its real-world experiences, while leaning into the creativity of humans in the process. After all, a visit to Galaxy’s Edge today will include actors dressed as characters, audio-animatronic robots, and even BDX droids, which are controlled by human operators.

“Ultimately the goal for Imagineering is to create a living world populated by all the characters you know and love,” Laughlin says. “Some of those are going to be audio-animatronics, some of those are going to be robots, some of those are going to be live performers, and some might be puppets. And I think our ability to blend all of those performances together is what makes us uniquely Disney and a one-of-one company in terms of delivering that kind of experience.”

We're scared of the Xenomorphs again, but Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 knows old-fashioned bug hunts shouldn't be a thing of the past.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games, and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel.

At Summer Game Fest 2026, we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong?

Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years.

Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2's pure survival horror to look forward to.

Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason.

Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat.

This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running.

All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode.

At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away.

There are still some scares hiding in here, though, ready to make complacent players jump out of their seats. Special Xenomorphs have tricks to pounce on distracted players, throwing chaos into the middle of their carefully coordinated rain of fire. Others have the ability to spit from afar, breaking tight defenses that count on the Xenos' predictable tactics from other games and the movies.

It's been 40 years since Aliens first graced the big screen, but Fireteam Elite 2 manages to refresh that mix of horror and action well enough, despite sharing much of its bones with the original game. But the disturbing lack of polish threatens to undo Cold Iron Studios' best ideas.

Those ideas include more varied enemies, which can disrupt almost any tried-and-tested team composition, and even a late-game class that rewards an extensive knowledge of the game by letting veterans pick weapons from all over the roster to create a custom loadout.

These playful creative swings somewhat offset the frustration caused by glitched objectives, enemy AI that often goes off the rails, and performance issues that have often given me flashbacks to its predecessor's worst moments on PS4. Sometimes, you can just tell when six extra months would've done a game a lot of good, and it's obvious that Fireteam Elite 2 will be in a much better place by spring.

That said, its loose and confident approach to design is rare to see when dealing with games that adapt well-established IPs like Alien.

Recent Star Wars games have achieved just that, and even if Fireteam Elite 2 misses some of its shots and has faced more initial trouble than the USCM's first incursion on LV-426, it's safe to say its heart and mind are in the right place. No one can take that away from the devs. Show me another modern Alien video game that allows you to zap Xenomorphs to death with a big cannon or to hold them off with combat drones.

We've seen developers win uphill battles before, and we know for a fact the huge Alien fandom is as enduring as the deadly extraterrestrials, so Daybreak and Cold Iron have a chance to turn things around and solidify Fireteam Elite 2 as the iterative but satisfying sequel it actually is.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is available now for PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. A Nintendo Switch 2 version is coming in 2027.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

#719. New York Knicks Star Josh Hart Inks Two-Book Deal With HarperCollins (Exclusive)

The NBA star will publish a memoir next year, and a children's book after that.

New York Knicks guard Josh Hart has inked a two-book deal with News Corp.’s HarperCollins, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

Hart will write a memoir, Live to Serve, which will be released in July of next year, and a children’s book, which will be released at a later date. The memoir will include Hart’s humor, faith, and heart, and will chronicle his college career at Villanova through this year’s NBA championship.

Senior VP & publisher Lisa Sharkey and senior VP & publisher Nancy Inteli negotiated U.S. and Commonwealth rights to the books with Anthony Mattero at CAA.

“I’m honored to be able to show readers how faith can shape the way they work, lead, compete, parent, and live their lives,” says Hart. “I’m writing for athletes and fans, but also for parents, coaches, young people, business leaders, and anyone who has felt overlooked or wondered whether the work happening outside the spotlight still matters. My faith journey means everything to me as a player, a parent, a husband, and a human and I’m excited to bring readers along with me so they too can Live to Serve.

“Josh Hart is the heartbeat of the New York Knicks. Whether he moves with the ball or without it, he serves his teammates and the greater good, and he gives glory to God first and foremost,” says Sharkey. “This book will inspire fans to learn more about Josh and will entertain them with his sense of humor, but most importantly, it will remind readers that on the court, a higher power always wins the game of life.”

“Josh brings the same incredible energy to storytelling that he brings to the court,” adds Inteli. “Like Josh himself, the picture book is full of warmth, humor, and especially heart. Families will want to read it again and again.”
