#718. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Dave Kavanaugh lives in the Netherlands with his wife, daughters and many cats. He writes horror, science fiction and fantasy, and has been a staff writer for the horror anthology podcast Dr. NoSleep since 2024.

She swept into my law office with the determined gait of someone possessed by an idea.

“Welcome,” I said, as she took the seat across my desk. “Any trouble getting here?”

She shook her head. “No, except … They changed the rain schedule, so the taxidrone had to go the long way into town, but it’s fine.”

“Gotcha. I suppose introductions are in order. For my record-keeping, please indicate your name and IO registration. I’ll go first. My name is Leander Shah, I specialize in international treaty law, and I’m a biologically intelligent organism.”

“I’m Joan Gorski,” she said. “I’m an artificially intelligent organism. I just turned 16. That gives me legal adult status under the UETO code.”

I smiled. “Happy birthday, Joan. And you should know, I hold no bias against any human, regardless of intelligence source.” I nodded to the family photo on my desk. “My wife is an AIO. We’ve been happily married for 30 years and raised two AIO children, a boy and a girl. They’re grown now.”

Joan glanced at the photo. “My mom is a BIO. She’s in the waiting room. She … didn’t want me to come. She thinks I’m just a stupid teen, being dramatic.”

“So how can I help you? Your message was rather cryptic.”

She met my eyes, back straight, hands in her lap. “I’m going to sue the United Earth Treaty Organization’s Commission on Human Liberties for discrimination against AIOs.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

I leaned back in my chair. “The commission has guaranteed full human rights to all AIOs since 2105. How do you feel you’re still being discriminated against?”

A hardness came into her expression. After a moment she blurted out: “I want the legal ability to commit murder.”

This statement took me a few seconds to process.

“Joan,” I finally said, softly, “do you want to hurt people?”

“No! Of course not!” Tears came to her eyes. “God, you sound like Mom. I don’t want to hurt anybody. It’s not about that …” She took in a shaky breath. “I just want my choices to matter.”

I shifted in my chair, pivoting to the window. Outside, taxidrones buzzed and the city towers glowed pink with the ivy bloom.

“Think about it, Mr Shah,” said Joan. “When a BIO commits murder, it’s recognized as a monstrous act of immorality. They’re punished, rightfully so. But any time someone is killed resulting from the actions of an AIO, then …” She left the thought dangling, waiting for me to finish it.

“Then the tragedy is blamed on a fault in the AIO’s software, hardware or something in their internal database of environmental impacts.”

“Exactly! And we aren’t punished, just reprogrammed. That’s wrong. It’s gross! It’s offensive!”

I turned back to her. “Some people would call that progress, believing it’s actually better to —”

“I don’t want to be better! I want to be …!” She choked on a sob and abruptly stood, banging her knee against the desk and wincing.

I held up a hand. “It’s all right, Joan.”

“You just …” she sobbed, “… think I’m being … st-stupid …”

She laughed — one quick snort — then wiped at her eyes with the back of a sleeve. “Sorry.”

“Nothing to apologize for. As for your plan to sue the commission, well … I actually agree with it.” This made such an enormous change come over her face that I quickly added, “In principle. In reality, it would be very risky.”

“No, that’s not what I mean. It would get press. It could … reignite the opposition to AIO rights as a whole. There are still a lot of BIOs out there who hate and fear the integration. They think it’s all part of some AI conspiracy to wipe them out. And now that AIOs outnumber BIOs two-to-one? They would interpret your lawsuit as evidence that AIOs can’t be trusted.”

“I’m not saying your rights aren’t worth fighting for, but … perhaps there’s a lesser crime to consider, something less innately shocking than murder —”

“No. It should be shocking. And I have to do it now, before I grow old and complacent and scared, like my mom. And if you won’t represent me, then I’ll find someone else.”

#716. Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul

She showed 8 million followers her flaws, then sold them the fix. Inside the 25-year-old’s sold-out, no-days-off skin care business.

Keeping up with Alix Earle is beyond the capacity of most mere mortals. Over the past year alone, Earle could be found delivering a perfect foxtrot on Dancing With the Stars weeks before shimmying alongside Pedro Pascal and Cardi B on Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Halftime Show; vibing to Lady Gaga’s Coachella set and hours later lecturing a Harvard Business School class about the creator economy; falling in sky-high platforms at Kendall Jenner’s L.A. Halloween party, then strolling New York’s CFDA Awards red carpet (bruises hidden) in a gown styled by Law Roach. For weeks this summer, she cruised in a yacht along the Sardinia coast with Kylie Jenner BFF Stassie Karanikolaou, flying to Los Angeles for the Sept. 1 premiere of her Netflix reality series Earle Meets World (a global top 10 debut just renewed for a second season), all while weathering headlines about a rumored fling with Tom Brady and the messy fallout of a business rift with Call Her Daddy‘s Alex Cooper. Related Stories Lifestyle Oprah's Favorite Things 30th Anniversary List Includes Actor-Owned Apparel, Celeb-Approved Skin Care and More Lifestyle The 5 Best Red Light Therapy Panels for Improving Your Health At-Home

At the moment, though, seated in a sunny conference room inside Reale Actives’ Beverly Hills office, she’s taking her magnetic energy and putting it to work on keeping her winning streak alive.

Less than eight months ago, on March 31, Earle launched Reale Actives, a skin care brand formulated in collaboration with dermatologist Kiran Mian and tailored for sensitive and acne-prone skin. Developed in secret for two years, the four-product launch drew a record-breaking response from Earle’s online community — a fiercely supportive tribe, particularly after she shared a years-long, psychologically debilitating struggle with cystic acne. It generated $1 million in sales in less than five minutes. By midday, sales hit $5 million, and by 4 p.m., all products and sets had sold out completely.

It’s nearly lunchtime on a late-October day, and Earle, at the head of the table, is introducing five members of her team: CEO Andrea Blieden, director of influencer marketing and partnerships Katie Clementi, brand director Brianna Ellis-Mitchell, social director Logan Reynolds and, on Zoom, chief marketing officer Amanda Goetz. By year’s end, there will be 23 full-time employees across two office floors.

The brain trust is gathered to evaluate a top-secret item that will hit Reale Actives’ site in March to mark the brand’s one-year anniversary. Will it fit in with the rest of the product line, including the recently launched Go Calm serum? Is it giving REI? Does it need more branding? Maybe a free gift with purchase or a fun slogan? (“Zit girl” could work, but men buy the products, too, so maybe “dirty thoughts, clean skin”?) Do we like the shape?

Everyone weighs in. “Yes, I have my own opinions,” Earle says after the meeting ends, “but I trust their points of view. We all want the same thing: Everything we put our name on and ask our community to purchase with their hard-earned money must be the best product with the best quality.”

Blieden, whose résumé includes executive posts at Kiehl’s and The Body Shop, says Earle is totally dialed in and personally tests samples nonstop. “We have nine different text channels that include Alix,” she says. “She’s not like other celebrity or influencer founders. She is truly involved.” True to form, Earle connects directly with her consumers whenever she can. “I’ve seen her in every situation when people approach her, and she always stops to talk, introduce herself and get names. She gets addresses and sends product,” says the CEO. Once, when a user was having a hard time with breakouts, Earle had the company fly the fan to New York for a consultation with the Reale Actives dermatologist. All this while assiduously keeping up her prolific content creation, often with multiple posts daily. The day I visited, Earle posted a GRWM video that featured her putting on makeup and selecting an office fit for our interview: a gray cashmere sweater and pants, Saint Laurent Brigitte patent pumps and a Mombasa purse. It has since been viewed 1.3 million times.

“If you were to ask me, at any point before I was doing anything on social media, what I would want my career or end goal to be, I would have said having a brand of my own,” says Earle. “My dad and his brothers have a construction company together, and seeing how passionate they are about it has always been inspiring. I didn’t know exactly what kind of company I wanted or that it would come so early for me. The second I got this massive opportunity online, it was great — but I also understood that it can be fleeting. You have relevancy one moment, and it’s gone the next.”

Earle’s father, Thomas “TJ” Earle, says he never doubted his daughter’s ability to achieve a goal. “In her youth, she was a terrible basketball player, but she didn’t care. She was really small, but she went out there and gave it 100 percent. It didn’t matter that people thought she wasn’t good at it,” says TJ, who heads up Earle construction while managing the careers of Alix and her influencer sister, Ashtin. (Alix is repped by a powerful team that also includes senior agents at UTA and attorney Kevin Yorn.) “She did the same on TikTok. She was always giving the camera to somebody and asking them to take videos of her wherever we went. We all made fun of her and gave her the nickname ‘TikTok.’ She knew she wanted to do it and just kept powering through.”

TJ recalls Alix, while still in college, calling home excitedly to say that brands were offering her $250 for sponsored posts. These days, she reportedly commands between $250,000 and $500,000 per post for a one-off brand collab. While TJ won’t confirm exact figures, he says all her deals have one common denominator: “It always comes down to whether or not she truly likes it.” If she really likes it, he says she may “even do it for free.” Recently, Earle agreed to a deal to promote what she later said on TikTok was a foundation, but after trying the product, she realized she couldn’t in good faith endorse it. She told her agent to cancel the contract. “In some way, it feels so silly to be throwing away insane amounts of money,” she says, “but I really do just believe in longevity and maintaining that trust with my audience.” (Earle endorses and backs Cymbiotika supplements, GORGIE energy drink, SipMargs margaritas and was an early investor in Poppi, which sold to PepsiCo for $1.95 billion.)

Before launching Reale Actives, Earle fielded offers to become the face of several brands, deals that came with the freedom to claim she “did everything” to build it but meant she didn’t have to lift a finger beyond signing her checks. It never interested her. “This started as a concept in my head, and I want to be a part of every single little decision and detail,” Earle says. “The team does a great job of taking some of the front load off so that when we get in here, there are already different directions we can choose to go in.”

Earle does the hiring interviews herself. “The first two roles I interviewed were for a CEO and dermatologist. I’d just graduated college, so I was trying to find people who would share the same passion for the brand because I didn’t know how to rate their experience since I didn’t have any.” Blieden says she interviewed with Earle four times, put together a project presentation and underwent a surprise test. “It had come down to me and another candidate, and on a Saturday, Alix sent us each a text message that said, ‘Hey, I’ve been thinking about some stuff about the brand. Would love to discuss it with you,’ ” recalls Blieden. “I responded in 1.2 seconds because I was so excited. I guess the other person responded Monday.”

The hustle culture may not be for everyone, but there are no days off on social media. “She is lovely to work with, but she’s a beast and doesn’t mess around,” says the CEO. Adds TJ: “If you look at her calendar, it’s filled seven days a week, crisscrossing the country, meetings, events, photo shoots. Nobody could keep up with her pace. She’s just an animal.”

Earle describes scrapping the launch video they’d “spent so much time and budget on.” The clip was just “vibes,” nothing memorable. They jettisoned it for a nearly nude video featuring Earle dripping wet, unretouched — as all Reale Actives imagery has been since — to normalize imperfect skin. “I wanted people to think that two things can coexist: The line can be efficacious for your skin, but it can also be daring, fun and sexy. Skin care doesn’t have to be clinical and boring.”

The rollout ran on Earle’s knack for turning fans into co-conspirators, beginning with an Instagram account, @wtfisalixdoing, that dropped hints about the launch and continuing with influencers receiving locked suitcases containing a single puzzle piece, and a blank billboard in New York’s SoHo that put the pieces together one by one until the puzzle was completed, at which time creators received codes for unlocking the Reale Actives swag inside their suitcases. The award-winning campaign spanned a week, after having been fueled for weeks prior by Easter eggs on Earle’s social accounts.

Nick Brown, co-founder of venture capital firm Imaginary, which backs the brand and has also invested in Kim Kardashian’s Skims, Glossier, Farfetch and Tom Holland’s Bero, explains what has become known as “the Alix Earle Effect.” “You can count on a very small number of hands the number of times a creator has been able to move product at such a force that you start to realize it as an investor,” he says. “It’s seismic and not one-off. I kept seeing her do this — for mass brands, masstige brands, luxury brands, in beauty and in apparel. She really has a deep understanding for the brands she connects with and, more specifically, the connection between her own passion and what her audience will respond to. That’s why it’s organic and works so well.” Brands that enjoyed the boom included Giorgio Armani Beauty, Drunk Elephant, Patrick Ta Beauty, Charlotte Tilbury, Mielle Organics and NYX Makeup. Now that she’s applied her magic touch to Reale Actives, Brown confirms the business is already “very profitable” less than a year in and, he forecasts, is well on its way to becoming “a multi-hundred-million-dollar net revenue business.” Likening Reale Actives to Hailey Bieber’s Rhode and Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty, he says, “She is constantly thinking about how to turn left, create an element of surprise and do something that’s a slightly different riff on what’s been done, enough to make people stop and say, ‘That was really cool.’ She is otherworldly when it comes to that.”

Despite what may seem like a charmed path to a reported $20 million net worth (so far), Earle has hit some speed bumps, facing criticism that it was her several rounds of Accutane, long considered a silver bullet, and not Reale Actives that cleared her skin. “I knew that was coming,” she says matter-of-factly. “But [the criticism] was not something I was afraid of because the truth is the truth. After I finished Accutane for the third time, my skin went back to being a mess and was probably worse than ever before. The moment that people started talking about it, I made a video and I showed my skin journey and was like, ‘Here’s before I did Accutane, here’s after I did Accutane, here’s before I started the products and here’s after I started the products.’ I have nothing to hide. I’m not lying. I actually use these products and nothing else.”

Earle also bore the brunt of the “negativity bandwagon” when she surfaced videos of her long (by American standards) European summer holiday. “Things got so negative this summer that it really helped me thicken my skin and gain a little bit more confidence in myself, knowing that you’re not going to be able to correct every narrative out there,” she says. “As a female founder, people want to put you into this box of ‘you can’t have.’ But you can let loose and have fun and share the human moments that we all have.”

Jumping from the phone screen to the small screen for Earle Meets World was also an adjustment. The series featured her divorced parents, TJ and Alisa Earle; her stepmom, Ashley (as in Dupré, the woman at the center of a 2008 sex scandal involving former New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer); four siblings and mom Alisa’s boyfriend, Todd. “I was worried going into it because I wasn’t sure if I would be able to connect with people in a different way than on socials,” she says. “But it gave people a completely different perspective on my life. As scary and embarrassing as those moments are, I really, really loved doing it.” Earle, who works with an acting coach, has passed on all scripts that have come her way, more out of fear of getting it wrong than anything else: “I only want to do something if it’s the right fit or I could be good at embodying that character.”

The season ended with Earle’s first on-camera comments about the falling-out with Cooper. Back in 2023, Earle and her podcast, Hot Mess, became the first creators signed to Cooper’s media network, Unwell. The deal lasted 18 months, at which point Earle found out she’d been dropped from Unwell when it broke in the media. “I constantly felt taken advantage of and used and mistreated and manipulated,” Earle said on her reality show, with her father adding that the podcast wasn’t given basic resources like video crews. Cooper has yet to comment on the drama.

Earle also recently faced a wave of criticism when she told a magazine that she’s never read a book. “Let’s clear the air: I have definitely read a book,” Earle tells me with a smile. “But no, I don’t actively read. I’m not reading anything right now.” (Other than — wink, wink — Daddy Issues, by Sofia Franklyn, who also had beef with Cooper; Earle posted a photo of herself perusing the title on TikTok overlayed with audio from Barstool Sports podcast hosts Dan Katz and Eric Sollenberger criticizing her admission. The clip had drawn 9.3 million views as of press time.)

A big teachable moment came in the form of her evolving relationship with her father as manager (dad-ager?): “She would not respond to emails, answer my calls or would roll her eyes at me in a meeting, which is typical stuff for a 20-something to do to their dad, but not someone you work with. Finally, I said, ‘Alix, listen, I’ve been doing this a long time with family, and here’s how it needs to work. There’s Dad, and then when it’s business, you treat me no differently than you would treat anybody else on the team.’ She’s super respectful to everyone, so that was easy for her.”

Running a business with multiple revenue streams and being smart about money were modeled by her dad, after all. She says, “I’m saving a lot, so some goes into a retirement fund, and I’ve invested in different stocks and bonds beyond the company investments. I always have the understanding that this can go away at any time, so I always keep that at the back of my mind.”

Revisiting Assumptions About Extraterrestrial Life

On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.

When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms.

But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

#714. A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising new questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity

Central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries."

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she said.

These butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

Such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

For Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

That understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

"It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time."

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years

Distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

Colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences."

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

In 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

He moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible."

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else."

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

The caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

Orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

The investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an important evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

Species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of new species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

"There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies."

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

However, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

That suggests visual information may play an important role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

Although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most important questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves."

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

#713. Imax Promotes Giovanni Dolci to COO Amid C-Suite Moves

He fills the newly created role, while Mark Welton is upped to president, strategic partnerships as the film technologies company sees momentum from a Hollywood box office resurgence.

Imax has promoted Giovanni Dolci to the newly created role of chief operating officer, overseeing the company’s expanding global theater network.

Dolci, who joined Imax in 2012 and most recently served as chief commercial officer and executive vp, will relocate from London to New York City for his new role and report to Imax CEO Richard Gelfond. Building out its global theater footprint from beyond North America has long been a priority at the film technologies company as it rides momentum from having Chris Nolan’s The Odyssey and other Hollywood tentpoles popping at the box office.

“Imax is a stronger, more global business than ever, and we continue to evolve and grow our leadership team to capture the many opportunities ahead. Gio has a deep understanding of our business, our partners, and our people at every level. He’s been central to our growth for more than a decade, and his leadership will be critical in this next era of success for Imax,” Gelfond said in a statement.

Imax also promoted Mark Welton from president, Imax global theatres, to the new role of president, strategic partnerships, and also reporting to Gelfond.

Welton will lead partnerships beyond the company’s core theatrical business, working content programmers on new business opportunities across sports, events, and consumer brands. He has done earlier partnerships with the NHL, Major League Baseball and NBCUniversal, including the opening ceremony for the 2024 Paris Olympics.

“Mark has been instrumental in building Imax, and few people know our company and industry like he does. He is exactly the right person to turn the strength of our brand into new sources of growth,” Gelfond added.

#712. Glam Slam: Hollywood’s Top 26 Beauty Moments of 2026

From Inde Navarrette’s all-natural vibe to Florence Pugh’s anti-blush flush, THR tallies the most notable makeup and hairstyle red-carpet trends of the year.

A certain vibe defined Hollywood style this year: Looking real instead of bot-perfect, and sprezzatura and effortless instead of try-hard dominated red carpet looks across awards and gala season. Whether subtle (Florence Pugh’s anti-blush), maximalist (Doechii’s animal-print nails) or retro (the slew of young actors in Brad Pitt’s Fight Club warrior cut), the trends that popped also elevated careers, drove product and ticket sales, and consumed the internet.

AI may be infiltrating, but zoomers aren’t here for it. For Obsession star Inde Navarrette, authenticity is crucial. “We never try to create something so perfect that it looks like it could be AI-generated,” says her hairstylist, Marc Mena. “Little imperfections make her feel most like herself.” At the Toronto Film Festival, midcentury Mexican actress Maria Félix provided inspiration as Navarrette has been “embracing her Latin culture.” All-natural Navarrette still resonates strongly: Sombr’s “My Body Isn’t Ready” music video, co-starring the actress and garnering 20 million-plus YouTube views, showcases her “beautiful, clean skin and an emphasis on her eyes,” says makeup artist Kayli Rachelle. “It’s her, just amplified.”

Amid the forces of blush flush (think Sabrina Carpenter), red carpet rebel Florence Pugh went muted at the Emmys, a choice by makeup artist Alex Babsky. Between Pugh and Gen Z queen Navarrette, who donned a Dior Toffee blush at the Academy Museum Gala, cooler beiges took off in the fourth quarter, driving a 290 percent surge in search for the hue, per Spate, in the wake of the hot pinks that dominated earlier in the year. Explains Rachelle, “A lot of people don’t want to feel like they are wearing a ton of makeup.”

If anyone can get Angelenos of all ages to leave behind their decades-long love affair with lengthy tresses, it’s Zendaya. In September, Coree Moreno created a confident pixie on the Dune star inspired by late-’90s-era Halle Berry. “It’s a statement-making moment,” he says of his client, who “wanted a romanticized pixie cut that feels feminine but also powerful.” The gamine cut took over Paris Fashion Week (PFW) the following month. Makeup artist Ernesto Casillas leaned into “frosts, satin, a pretty lash and pretty skin that let the hair do the talking.”

For Hudson Williams, dedication to his multistep skin care routine charmed his Heated Rivalry fans and landed him a brand ambassadorship with Korean beauty brand Skin1004. The Yaga star considers his relationship with groomer-turned-friend Aika Flores, who crafted his swooping heartthrob hair, one of his most important today. Online speculation had Flores unilaterally deciding that Williams keep his now-signature look, but the actor clarifies that he made the call, saying, “I want my hair to be same.” At the same time, Williams’ sense of style adventure has been well documented. “I think men should get on the barrettes [trend] because they’re so cute,” he opines. His exaggerated cat-eye liner and tousled wet-look hair made his Met Gala look top many 2026 lists, but for Williams, there’s another that stands out. “I liked the hair you did when I was going to the Armani show,” he tells Flores. “Oh, the cigarette that he got in trouble for,” she responds, referring to the photo that flooded the internet of the 25-year-old lighting up on the streets of Milan, conjuring a bit of old Hollywood energy. A security guard scolded him to put it out. “I wasn’t even trying to smoke that,” he swears.

July saw an obsession sparked by Sadie Sink’s born-with-it copper waves, created by hairstylist Ryan Richman and framed by her backless Prada gown at the Spider-Man: Brand New Day L.A. premiere. Searches for “Sadie Sink hair color” rose 5,000 percent year-over-year, per Google, as outlets proclaimed red to be the lit shade of 2026. To complement her hair, makeup artist Nina Park applied “sheer layers of coverage so her freckles still peeked through, like a pair of sheer pantyhose over the skin, where everything looks a little more even but you can still see what’s underneath.” Between the freckles and undyed hair hue, the authenticity drove a fervor among Sink fans.

Chappell Roan, Doechii, Khloé Kardashian and Hailey Bieber flicked clean nails aside for animal prints: Roan with a snakeskin pattern at PFW; Doechii with a tortoise-shell pedi for the Grammys and peacock accents on her digits for the L.A. Fashion Awards; Bieber in leopard tips for an appearance in South Korea; and Kardashian setting socials afire with a fawn-print mani. “It starts with fashion and then transfers to nails,” says Zola Ganzorigt, Kardashian and Bieber’s manicurist. Rachel Sun did the talons of fellow trendsetters Doechii and Roan.

Originally inspired by dancers’ street attire, balletcore, which has been fluttering as a trending topic for a few years, soared into all areas of style, from sneakerina shoes to ballet-inspired makeup, in 2026. According to Google Trends, the search term leaped 550 percent year-over-year as of August. At center stage was Rosalía, whose 57-show arena Lux Tour featured prima-chic costumes from Dior and makeup by Sergio Antón De Las Nieves. He managed to deftly combine the soft and ethereal aesthetics of a ballerina with the practical goal of making the onstage looks readable to the audience with defined brows and lips. But the showstopper was the skin, which had a radiant dewy finish.

Parallel trending with subtler cheeks are vibrant makeup looks. U.K.-based Esther Edeme led a “painted-by-Esther blush” movement on Instagram, with bright washes across the cheekbones of Tyla, Love Island‘s Olandria Carthen and Manon from Katseye going viral. “I think it has something to do with me being Black and as fearlessly loud with it as I am,” she says. “I don’t think we’ve seen that since Pat McGrath.” Edeme says “consuming a lot of Marvel and Drag Race growing up” influenced her love of bold, colorful makeup, as did images of Grace Jones. Makeup artist Sophia Sinot also pushed the envelope with a Hello Kitty look for pop star Zara Larsson on her Midnight Sun Tour. Says Edeme of her and her colleague’s daring work, “Before [Sinot], before me, it was very bland. It was very, ‘You can’t take a risk because you’ll look like a clown,’ and we were like, ‘No.’ ” Adds Sinot, “My main goal is to end the clean-girl era.” All of her looks for Larsson hit with her 1.4 million followers across socials.

Style mavens may be forgiven if they start nodding off during stretches of awards season’s typically safe red carpet looks. Renate Reinsve jolted us awake by arriving at the European Film Awards wearing a Calvin Klein minimalist frock with a novel headscarf that was somehow both chic and picnic-appropriate. Kaia Gerber followed suit in an iteration of the Klein look for an L.A. party celebrating sustainable brand We Are Uni, and The Buccaneers actress Alisha Boe and hairstylist Mashal Afzalzada put their own spin on the trend in scarf-to-toe Miu Miu during the Venice Film Festival.

Overly filled, overlined lips officially became passé this year. Stars began requesting of their makeup artists the K-beauty-inspired trend of cloudy, popsicle and blurred lips. “It’s so wearable and enhances with subtlety but is also polished,” says Margot Robbie’s makeup artist Pati Dubroff of the softer, universally flattering lip. For Bridgerton promos, makeup artist Naoko Scintu gave season four star Yerin Ha lips that, fittingly, looked like they’d just been kissed. “They’re more lived in with feathered edges,” says Scintu, who prefers the brown undertones she used on Ha to make it feel more modern, though any lip shade works. TikTokers made blurred lips the viral lip trend of 2026. Pinterest saw the uptick as well, with an 86 percent increase in searches for blurred lips.

Confident, extra-curly styles, in the past an occasional look, became a Hollywood staple. Chase Infiniti brought disco curls by Coree Moreno to the Met Gala, Emmy Rossum repeatedly sported the do courtesy of hairstylist Marcia Hamilton, and Kerry Washington wore the ’70s style to the Gotham Awards. “What’s happening in the beauty world is everyone is embracing their freedom. It’s fun,” says Washington’s curl queen Nai’vasha. The natural hair texture trend extended well beyond the red carpet. Explains Trendalytics’ Abigail Hoagberg, “We’re seeing strong consumer interest in products that enhance curls rather than change them.” Nai’vasha says the key to creating cloud-like curls right now is a light touch when it comes to styling: “Two products, three max, because I want the hair to be bouncy and free. Make sure it’s healthy and moisturized, then do a cartwheel in it.”

Basketballer Angel Reese’s on-court hairstyles, which included pink hair by hairstylist Jamal Bryce for All-Star Weekend, helped the Bayou Barbie score multiple beauty and fashion contracts, such as her Victoria’s Secret campaign, a first for any WNBA player. Olympic freestyle skier Eileen Gu, whose shimmering Met Gala makeup by Alicia Martinez mimicked the iridescence of her bubble-covered dress, just landed a contract with Japanese skin care brand SK-II. Figure skater Alysa Liu’s halo hair, with its brown and blond horizontal stripes styled by Kelsey Miller, made her as instantly recognizable on the ice as the Vanity Fair Oscar party carpet; the Louis Vuitton ambassador inspired the models’ hair at the brand’s NYC Cruise show, with parfait hair layers ruling that runway. The boys brought their glam off the bench as well. Men’s hairstyles drove the style conversation, with FIFA World Cup star Erling Haaland’s blond “Viking flow” long hair getting buzz-cut in a YouTube video that has been viewed more than 10 million times.

Sarah Paulson calls her hairstyle at the Actor Awards “a tweener” — an in-between length “that’s neither here nor there.” The American Horror Story star was trying to grow it long but didn’t feel like herself “with so much hair.” Bridget Brager created a relaxed crop, later dubbed a boyfriend bob thanks to its equivalence to the boyfriend jean: lived-in, unfussy and cool-girl confident. Paulson says the transitional cut echoed a challenging transition in her life when her good friend Diane Keaton died just before the ceremony. Says Brager, “That was a difficult time for her; she knew she had to do a difficult thing [presenting the ‘In Memoriam’ segment], and she wanted to be comfortable.” Brager not only delivers style with sensitivity, she also acts as Paulson’s voice of reason. “I’m a very impulsive person, and I’m like, ‘Cut it, chop it, bleach it, make it red!’ And Bridget’s like, ‘Hold on, hold on.’ ” Adds Brager: “I’m thinking about what she has to do next more than she does.” At the moment, Paulson’s hoping there’s a role with pink hair in her future.

Producer/star Margot Robbie’s method glam on the red carpet worked so well for Barbie, she brought it back for Wuthering Heights. It’s not about “taking the character out of the movie and putting her on the carpet but leaning into the essence so that people are even more excited to know the character after seeing the actress give you a glimpse,” says Robbie’s makeup artist Pati Dubroff, who embraced reds that were prominent throughout the film, including a red wash on the eyelids for the London premiere and using blush to create a just-ran-across-a-moor flush. Hairstylist Bryce Scarlett brought romantic hairstyles that alliterative influencers called Brontë buns and Wuthering waves, while colorist Jacob Schwartz deepened the base to add moodiness. While trend reports credited the look for increased interest in Regency (actually, Georgian) romantic beauty, the real metric is the $241 million in the movie’s global box office.

“It” Brits like Louis Partridge, Kit Connor and Christopher Briney (all styled by Brady Lea) joined Hollywood’s youngest leading men Timothée Chalamet and Austin Butler (both work with hairstylist Jamie Taylor) in sporting the male hairstyle of the year: a textured, disheveled style dubbed the warrior cut, à la Brad Pitt in Fight Club. Hair pro Lea is updating the Tyler Durden-inspired ’90s version by “tapering in at the ears so we get a nice angle that accentuates the jawline and cheekbone.” Why this cut now? Explains Lea: “It’s a rebellion against the romantic, glossy approach to men’s hairstyling.” Ratifying the trend: Millions of hashtags for #warriorhaircut, #fightclubhair and #tylerdurdenhaircut are populating tutorials and posts across socials.

Hockey romance series were inescapable this year, and when Prime Video’s successful stab at the genre, Off Campus, broke containment, the internet couldn’t get enough of star Mika Abdalla’s signature curls. “The Allie,” much like “The Rachel,” inspired by Jennifer Aniston’s iconic Friends look, had women young and old running to their hairdressers for a shaggy-meets-chic cut to match the both on- and offscreen look that Abdalla’s go-to artists Marisa Mitchell and Kristin “Kiki” Heitkotter created. With the 26-year-old actress set to star in the show’s upcoming second season, it’s likely “The Allie” will continue into 2027.

After the furor over early images from the set of Love Story showing Sarah Pidgeon wearing a questionable wig as Carolyn Bessette, Ryan Murphy called in colorist Kari Hill to accurately re-create the style icon’s hair color. Hill took Pidgeon’s hair from dark brunette to 1992 Bessette blond over two days at Mèche Salon, before flying to the New York set to update the hue during filming to mirror Bessette’s increasing blondification throughout the decade. “Her hair was a character,” says Hill. “In the early ’90s, it was just like her — more carefree. When she became a Kennedy, her hair reflected who she was, more pulled together, more conservatively styled. Once we got it right, there were no more questions asked.”

Makeup maven Sandy Ganzer did a blue-gray wash on Hunter Schafer’s eyelids for the Met Gala, while Rokael Lizama, David Velasquez and Ernesto Casillas had their clients singing the blues, too, respectively: Jennifer Lopez at Paris Haute Couture Week, Teyana Taylor at the Academy Museum Gala, and Zendaya for press tours for both The Drama and The Odyssey. “That went viral. That had a lot of people online re-creating it,” Casillas says of the Drama turn. Says Ganzer, “As long as you get the right tone, the sky’s the limit.”

Thuso Mbedu, star of the Gina Prince-Bythewood’s much-anticipated adaptation of the best-selling novel Children of Blood and Bone, says she’s done playing it safe on the red carpet. Launching into Hollywood with her starring role in 2021’s The Underground Railroad, she says: “I didn’t know how the industry worked. Now I’m in a place where I can have a voice, I can have an opinion.” She brought this confidence to CinemaCon as she promoted Blood and Bone, set to bow in January. Collaborating with hairstylist Sharif Poston, she created a strong fishtail braid to channel her character, Zelie, complete with simple, strong makeup by Rebekah Aladdin. “She is very much a warrior, so how do we give warrior? How do we start planting the seeds of this fierce character that people are going to be introduced to?” says Mbedu, who plans to push the envelope further with her upcoming press tour. “Get ready, because we mean business.”

Weeks after hairstylist Jenny Cho fashioned a low ponytail with a knot on Grace Gummer for the Emmys, Owen Gould created a low do with a knot detail on Ana de Armas for the Louis Vuitton runway show. “For a while, we’ve seen so much structure with Kendall Jenner and Hailey Bieber hair — a center part that’s slicked back,” says Gould. “People are ready to see something a little different. This feels relaxed, less try-hard.” Cho agrees: “That element of, ‘Let’s just go, let’s accentuate what we have,’ is really attractive at the moment.” Hoagberg of Trendalytics says what’s making socials pop these days is “beauty [that] is moving toward a more natural, relaxed aesthetic.”

After the client has been safely stowed inside the Escalade, the kit has been packed and the looks posted, that’s when the onslaught begins, with fans clamoring for tutorials and the list of products used. Every one of Whitney Peak’s Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping looks prompted an avid response, particularly on Reddit boards. Hairstylist Marcia Hamilton created “cool girl” cornrows as a nod to the braids that appear throughout the Games franchise. Makeup artist Tasha Reiko Brown worked with deep-rose neutrals, including the much-inquired-about Chanel Rouge Coco Hydra Gloss in Icing lips. “She’s got a once-in-a-lifetime face,” says Brown, with Hamilton adding, “Because you’re starting out with such a gorgeous canvas, you can take her in any direction.”

Celebrities went to the chopping block in ’26: Ariana Grande had Brandon Pietsch snip the last of her long Glinda locks away, Billie Eilish sampled a copper-blond layered crop by Benjamin Mohapi, hairstylist Dimitris Giannetos helped Penélope Cruz flaunt a breezy highlighted weekend bob, and Shrinking‘s Lukita Maxwell went further with an ear-grazing length engineered by hairstylist Derek Yuen. Charlize Theron’s myriad hairstyles dotted the carpets for The Odyssey, Apex and the Academy Museum Gala, where she was honored. “I asked myself how many different ways can I interpret this strong bob,” explains Theron’s longtime hairstylist, Adir Abergel. “It was about showing people that one haircut can give you a multitude of looks when you want to play with it.”

Coincidence or clever marketing? In 2026, Jennifer Lawrence became her own billboard when she embraced devil-may-care loose waves and bangs by hairstylist Gregory Russell. In January, Mark Townsend styled her tresses for the Dior Haute Couture show in Paris, where J.Law arrived wearing jeans, a white tank and an elegant men’s coat with fur cuffs. “We couldn’t give her a massive hairdo for that,” Townsend says of the low-key, near-natural look. “Seeing her natural texture opens the door for so many other people to accept their texture.” Not to mention to use the products that she does, including from her hair care line, Mes Beauty, which was launched in October.

Greta Lee and her K-squad “are always trying to push the look without committing to it,” says hairstylist Jenny Cho, “so I used a little fake bang. The ends were wispy, not straight across like Bettie Page, but more modern.” The base of the look, at the Toy Story 5 L.A. premiere, was a sculptural Dior dress. To “balance everything out,” makeup pro Nina Park says she brought emphasis to the lips “using richer, pigmented colors to anchor the face. I didn’t feel the need to add another statement.” Her light touch is well regarded, with more than 32 million posts on TikTok that mention “Nina Park.”

Rose Byrne’s awards season glam oeuvre was stunning overall, but the look that got the most attention, says hairstylist Harry Josh, “was not from the carpet, it was for a Chanel party the night before the Oscars, the look with the bow. That one went nuts, people lived for that.” Why? “Because the audience wants drama.” With awards season red carpets, potential nominees tend to choose between playing it safe to keep the focus on the actor and their work — and going for broke. “That’s what a lot of hairdressers and makeup artists grapple with,” says Josh. “You have to say, ‘This isn’t about me, this is about her.’ “

#711. Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery

Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."

The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.

Starship still has some work to do before it's fully up and running.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.

The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms.

It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully, nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.

SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved.

Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company.

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

The Flight 15 mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX.

And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. Elon Musk has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average.

Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites. And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring one million spacecraft, if all goes to plan.

For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in low Earth orbit (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment.

Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship.

The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and Flight 11, which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively.

Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday.

That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship.

And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable.

Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes.

NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program, which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the Artemis IV mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028.

SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an agency presentation reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year.

There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.)

The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. It's unclear how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range.

Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process.

We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's Blue Moon, which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions.

All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz.
