#709. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

#707. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

Crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent."

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

The dramatic brightening was caused by an outburst on the comet that dumped billions of pounds of dust into space.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times.

Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars. Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit), 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life.

On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event.

By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August.

Comets are often referred to as dirty snowballs, and beneath their dusty crust are ices made from various volatiles, including water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Solar heating, even at the distance of Mars, can cause these ices to rapidly sublimate into gases, and the pressure of the escaping gas rips the surface apart, spewing huge amounts of dust in to space.

Models based on observations of 220P’s outburst indicate that it spewed out between tens of billions and hundreds of billions of pounds’ worth of cometary dust that filled the comet’s coma, the diffuse 'atmosphere' that clings to the comet’s solid nucleus. The dust particles, which are just millionths of a meter across, expanded outwards from the comet at about 1,280 feet (390 meters) per second, scattering sunlight and causing the coma to substantially brighten.

"We have concluded that the comet detached localized parts of its crust, creating a dust-rich envelope that increased [the comet’s brightness by] 250 times in half a day," Josep M. Trigo-Rodríguez, of the Institut de Ciències de l’Espai and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia in Spain, said in a statement.

While this is the first time that 220P has been seen to outburst, over the years we have witnessed other comets spectacularly brighten out of nowhere.

A recent and well-known example is comet 17P/Holmes, which brightened a million-fold in the fall of 2007 as it rose from magnitude +17 to magnitude +2.8, becoming a welcome naked-eye sight in the constellation of Perseus for many people as they made the evening commute home.

The short 5.5-year orbit of 220P marks it out as a Jupiter-family comet.

"Jupiter-family comets are extremely interesting objects to study because they originate primarily from the Kuiper Belt and the Scattered Disk region, later migrating inward until Jupiter captures them into short-period orbits," said Trigo-Rodríguez.

Studying outbursts such as the two experienced by 220P provides vital clues as to the bulk characteristics of Jupiter-family comets, giving us insight into objects that originated from beyond the orbit of Neptune.

Of particular interest to Trigo-Rodríguez is what we should do were one of these objects ever to be found on a collision course with Earth.

"Particularly we are interested in the tensile strength and nature of comets in the framework of our studies on impact hazards," said Trigo-Rodríguez. "Some comets seem determined to demonstrate that they are fragile enough and perhaps give us the chance to invoke disruptive approaches that might be substantially different from the ones already tested or proposed for asteroids."

For now, 220P is heading back out to its furthest point from the sun, which is just inside the orbit of Jupiter at a distance of 4.68 astronomical units or 435 million miles (700 million kilometers). Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031.

The findings were published on Nov.3 in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#705. Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

For decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing new scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

The research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity

The discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely new explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

Einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

Earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

Akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive

The team's calculations showed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

One mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

What makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

The theory also avoids an important potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension

The new findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Big Bang.

Previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

However, an important question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

The latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

"For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself."

DESI Observations Raise New Questions About Dark Energy

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

These findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

The timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI announced its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an important next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

Because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

The extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

In this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Ultimately, the strength of the new explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

"We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.

Looking ahead to season two, Serena Williams shared that the podcast will feature more solo episodes and deeper discussions on important topics. “We’re going to dive into women’s health topics, and important conversations that people don’t normally have.” She added, “We’re bringing more educational things to the podcast. "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."

Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#702. Taylor Swift’s CMA Return Helped Disney Sell More Ads

Taylor Swift doesn’t work for the Walt Disney Company, but she may just have played a key role in helping the company carve out a little extra revenue.

Swift hasn’t performed on the Country Music Association Awards, televised on ABC, since 2013. On Friday, after the musician announced she would return to the program, Disney’s sales force opened some new streaming ad inventory tied to the event. Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad

“We were sold out.  We opened up additional opportunities because of Taylor, and we got additional interest, and we were seeing brands come in” all this week, says John Campbell, senior vice president of entertainment and streaming solutions at Disney Advertising, during a recent interview. “We can create demand 24 hours before the show.”

Such activity may be encouraging not only for Disney, but for the broader media sector, which is placing a growing emphasis on live events in a bid to keep the large audiences advertisers crave coming to its screens. Disney has in the last year put together a large schedule of sporting events and spectacles, including the CMAs, the College Football Playoffs, Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve, the Grammys and the 2027 telecast of the Super Bowl — a string of big-ticket events that come with a large amount of advertising time that needs to be monetized.

Disney’s Campbell says ad revenue tied to the CMAs is up 20% compared to 2025’s telecast, and cites Madison Avenue’s desire for tentpole extravaganzas that are different from the rest of the TV schedule, as well as growing interest in creating bespoke promotions for social media and streaming video, along with traditional TV.

General Motors’ Chevrolet is returning for its tenth year as a presenting sponsor of the program. Its vehicles will be seen during the program, and country music artist Zach Top will appear in moments that celebrate country music and military service, among other things. Top will give fans a behind-the-scenes look at the creation of some of the vignettes he’s in via ABC and CMA social channels.

In a new venture, retailer Bed Bath & Bodyworks will be the presenting sponsor of live CMAs coverage on TikTok. Country star Lauren Alaina and digital creator Haley Baylee will serve up real-time content to fans, including branded moments, host integrations, interactive polls, and social engagement opportunities. “We know that fans want to interact with the show in so many different ways,” says Campbell, who notes this new type of sponsorship “provides additional content and more value for fans.”

Financial-services provider Ally is also new to the program’s ad roster. A new campaign will feature entrepreneur and reality show star Kristin Cavallari, and will surface during the show, on social and streaming venues and via linear TV commercials.

Advertisers interested in live specials are eager “to go beyond just the 30-second spot,” says Campbell. He believes new opportunities that weave marketing alongside musical content is driving “increases in overall commitments to our live specials.” There are, Disney no doubt hopes, a lot more to come.

#701. The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

In May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible. But the spectacular displays were only the most obvious signs of an enormous disturbance unfolding in space around Earth. Deep within the planet's magnetosphere, the vast region controlled by its magnetic field, scientists were witnessing something they had never directly measured before.

The event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession. As enormous clouds of magnetized plasma raced through space, they combined before slamming into Earth's magnetosphere. The resulting storm produced the strongest magnetic disturbance ever measured in Earth's ring current, a vast region of electrically charged particles surrounding the planet.

For decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from. Two major sources are known: the solar wind, which carries charged particles outward from the Sun, and Earth's ionosphere, an electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere. Both typically supply particles during geomagnetic storms, and some scientists expected the solar wind to remain an important contributor during an extreme event involving particularly dense solar wind.

Instead, the first direct measurements of ring current composition during a storm of this magnitude revealed something remarkable. Particles originating from the solar wind contributed very little, while those coming from Earth's own atmosphere dominated to an extent never previously observed.

Published in Science Advances, the findings suggest that Earth's atmosphere may play a much greater role in determining the severity of extreme geomagnetic storms than scientists previously recognized. Because the dominant ions from Earth are much heavier than the particles supplied by the solar wind, they may have strengthened the magnetic disturbance and caused the ring current to reach its greatest intensity unusually close to the planet.

The discovery also strengthens the case for a proposed Japanese satellite mission designed to investigate how atmospheric particles enter space and influence powerful geomagnetic storms.

How the May 2024 Solar Superstorm Disrupted Earth's Magnetic Field

On May 10 and 11, 2024, enormous clouds of charged solar particles struck Earth's magnetosphere, triggering one of the most powerful geomagnetic storms in decades. Known as the "Gannon storm" or "Mother's Day storm," the event pushed the SYM-H index, a measure of geomagnetic disturbance, to a minimum of −518 nanotesla. This represented the second-largest recorded disturbance since 1981. The previous storm of comparable strength occurred in November 2004.

Although the colorful auroras drew worldwide attention, the consequences of such storms can extend far beyond the night sky.

"Some super or extreme geomagnetic storms are not just impressive light shows -- they pose radiation risks to spacecraft, disturb GPS signals and communications, and cause power outages. Understanding how a geomagnetic storm develops is not only a scientific question, but also one with real-world consequences," said Naritoshi Kitamura, lead author and designated assistant professor from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

A major source of these magnetic disturbances is Earth's ring current. This enormous belt of energetic charged particles, primarily oxygen and hydrogen ions, slowly circulates around the planet thousands of kilometers above the equator.

As the ions move, they create an electrical current that generates its own magnetic field. That field partly opposes Earth's natural magnetic field, weakening the magnetic field measured at ground level. The resulting changes are among the key signals scientists use to track the strength of geomagnetic storms.

Japanese Satellite Reveals an Unexpected Source of Storm Particles

Scientists were able to investigate the May 2024 storm in unusual detail thanks to Japan's Arase satellite, which was launched in 2016 and is operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). The ERG (Arase) science center is jointly operated by the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS)/JAXA and the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research/Nagoya University.

Arase travels through the region of space where Earth's ring current forms. Its scientific instruments can measure both the mass and energy of individual ions, allowing researchers to determine the types of particles present during a storm.

By remarkable timing, the spacecraft passed through the ring current shortly after the May 2024 storm began and again as the disturbance approached its peak. These observations provided a rare opportunity to examine the composition of the ring current during an exceptionally powerful geomagnetic event.

"This is the first simultaneous observation of ring current ions and solar wind during a storm this large, and the data was clear -- approximately 85% of ions were oxygen from Earth's own ionosphere," Kitamura explained.

The overwhelming contribution from Earth's atmosphere was particularly surprising because the storm had been triggered by dense streams of material arriving from the Sun. Rather than supplying most of the ring current ions, the solar wind played a relatively minor role in the measured particle population.

The Arase measurements revealed another extraordinary feature of the storm. The magnetic field weakened dramatically in a region much closer to Earth than where similarly severe reductions had previously been documented.

"Near the peak of the storm, Arase detected a 40% decrease in magnetic field intensity at roughly 16,000 kilometers above Earth, and much closer to Earth than similar large decreases previously documented."

At the same time, the satellite detected a decline in the number of energetic electrons that normally circulate through this region of space.

Such an extreme weakening of the magnetic field can alter the paths followed by these electrons, causing them to drift away from their usual orbits. However, scientists have not yet determined whether the deformation of the magnetic field directly caused the observed electron loss. Further research will be needed to establish that connection.

Together, the observations provide new insight into how the ring current behaves during especially intense geomagnetic storms. They also suggest that the unusually large population of heavy ions originating from Earth's atmosphere may have helped produce the severe magnetic disturbance so close to the planet.

A New Clue to Predicting Dangerous Solar Storms

The findings could have important implications for space weather forecasting. Current models rely heavily on conditions in the solar wind to estimate how powerful an approaching geomagnetic storm might become.

However, the new measurements suggest that conditions within Earth's own upper atmosphere could also influence a storm's eventual intensity. Understanding how many atmospheric ions escape into the magnetosphere, and how they contribute to the ring current, may therefore be essential for making more reliable predictions.

The researchers believe that additional satellite observations could help answer these questions. Their findings support FACTORS, a proposed mission involving two satellites that is being prepared for an upcoming JAXA proposal opportunity.

FACTORS would investigate the processes that allow ions from Earth's atmosphere to flow into the magnetosphere and examine how those particles contribute to the development of geomagnetic storms.

By revealing how Earth's atmosphere and incoming solar material interact during extreme events, the mission could eventually improve forecasts of dangerous space weather. More accurate predictions would help scientists better anticipate storms capable of disrupting satellites, navigation systems, communications networks, and power infrastructure.

Materials provided by Nagoya University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.

When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.

Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.

"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus."

The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.

During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.

"One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#698. NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks

Organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important new piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life. Even more surprising, the material was found just beneath the planet's surface, where harsh conditions can destroy organic compounds.

The discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature. A potential biosignature is a substance or feature that could have formed through biological activity, although other explanations are possible. Now, research published in Science Advances provides definitive confirmation that the same two rocks, located in Mars' Bright Angel formation, contain organic carbon, an essential component of life. The findings also offer a clearer picture of the material's characteristics and how it may have been preserved.

The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.

NASA's Perseverance Rover Detects Complex Organic Carbon

To investigate the rocks, researchers used the Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument mounted on Perseverance's robotic arm. The instrument examined several rocks in the Bright Angel formation within Jezero crater, where the rover also collected a sample from a rock named "Cheyava Falls."

SHERLOC uses a technique called Raman spectroscopy, which shines laser light onto a material to identify and map its minerals and organic compounds without damaging the rock.

The measurements revealed macromolecular carbon (MMC), a form of carbon consisting of large, interconnected networks of carbon atoms. This type of material is also found in rocks on Earth and in meteorites. Importantly, it can form through biological activity or through chemical processes that do not involve life, so its presence alone cannot establish that Mars was once inhabited.

The surrounding geology offers additional clues about how the material reached these rocks. Billions of years ago, water flowed through a river channel into Jezero crater, carrying sediment that gradually settled on the bottom. Over time, those fine particles hardened into the mudstone formations Perseverance is now exploring.

Researchers detected the carbon within these ancient sediments and alongside carbonate and sulfate minerals that developed later as water altered the rocks. This distribution raises the possibility that organic material entered or formed within the rocks during at least two separate periods of Mars' geological history.

"While the specific formation mechanism of the MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones remains unknown, this is still one of the most exciting findings to date," Murphy said.

Organic Carbon Survives Just Beneath Mars' Harsh Surface

One of the most striking results concerns where the organic carbon was found. The material survived only a few microns below the exposed Martian surface, at a depth smaller than the thickness of a sheet of paper. This is the shallowest detection of macromolecular carbon ever reported on Mars.

That location makes the finding particularly unusual. Mars' surface is exposed to radiation, sunlight, and chemically reactive substances that can break down organic molecules. Scientists would generally expect these conditions to make long-term preservation especially difficult so close to the surface.

"The Martian surface environment includes radiation and chemical oxidants that are destructive to organics, and terrestrial laboratory simulations have shown that the survival time of organics in Martian-like conditions -- especially at or near the surface -- depends on factors such as the type of organic molecule and the surrounding minerals," Murphy said. "The MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones is either resistant to degradation and/or has been sufficiently shielded by other minerals, such as clays, or iron-rich Martian soil."

In other words, the carbon may have survived because of its own chemical durability, protection provided by surrounding minerals, or a combination of the two. Understanding how it endured could help scientists determine where similar organic compounds might remain preserved elsewhere on Mars.

Ancient Martian Lakes and Rivers May Have Been Rich in Organic Material

The findings also suggest that organic carbon may not have been confined to a single region of ancient Mars.

Perseverance collected the Bright Angel sample more than 2,000 miles from Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover previously detected organic compounds. Finding organic material at such widely separated locations suggests that the chemistry associated with life's building blocks may once have been common across the Martian landscape.

"It is encouraging for Martian habitability," Murphy said. "This indicates that billions of years ago, organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient lakes and rivers on Mars."

The possibility of widespread organic material is significant because ancient Mars once had environments containing liquid water. If organic compounds were also broadly available, some of those lakes and rivers may have offered important chemical ingredients for life.

However, discovering those ingredients does not mean that living organisms were present. Organic carbon can be produced without biology, and scientists still need to determine exactly how the material in the Bright Angel rocks formed.

Could Martian Rocks Preserve Evidence of Ancient Life?

Determining whether the Bright Angel formation contains fossilized microorganisms remains beyond the capabilities of the rovers currently exploring Mars. Neither Curiosity in Gale Crater nor Perseverance in Jezero Crater carries the large, energy-intensive laboratory equipment needed to conclusively distinguish fossil evidence of ancient life from geological processes.

Perseverance was designed to search for potential biosignatures, including features like those identified in the Cheyava Falls rock. From that perspective, the discovery represents a "resounding win for Mars science," Murphy said.

The next major step would be to examine Martian samples using the more sophisticated instruments available in laboratories on Earth. Such equipment could reveal details too small or chemically subtle for the rover's instruments to resolve, helping researchers determine whether biological processes or nonliving chemistry produced the organic carbon.

If samples from the Bright Angel formation eventually reach Earth, scientists hope to study their minerals and organic compounds with much greater sensitivity and resolution. These investigations could help explain how the macromolecular carbon formed, how it survived, and what its presence reveals about the distribution of organic material across Mars.

Murphy continues to collaborate with the SHERLOC science team as Perseverance explores the Martian surface. Her research also includes studying Earth materials that resemble Martian rocks and using Raman spectroscopy to improve how scientists interpret the measurements returned by the rover.

Murphy's work on SHERLOC Instrument Mars 2020 was supported through JPL Subcontract No. 1641753 to the Planetary Science Institute.

#697. DOC NYC Doc ‘Dryads,’ From Mallorca-Based Miguel Eeks, Explores ‘the Mystery of Creation Through Music’

Competing at prominent documentary fest DOC NYC, which also hosts its international premiere, Miguel Eek’s “Dryads” (“Dríades”) ponders the mystery of musical creation as he follows three indie musicians, Vasco Ribeiro from Portugal, Joana Gomila in Mallorca and Norway’s Emil Karlsen, as they source their music from their environs and local traditions.

Produced by Mallorca-based Mosaic, “Dryads” focuses on the creative process behind their works: Karlsen, a young Sámi musician and multi-instrumentalist, seeks inspiration for his joiks, the time-honored songs of his culture, in the fjords and tundra of northern Norway; Gomila explores the acoustic mysteries of caves, abandoned buildings and the expressive possibilities of the human voice, while Ribeiro, also known as Omiri, reworks traditional Portuguese music into something more modern and uniquely his own. Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad

Despite their different approaches, all three share a common curiosity: how music comes into being, and how tradition, experimentation, improvisation and individual expression come together to create something new.

Through “Dryads,” Eek continues his exploration of observational cinema and its capacity to capture human experience through intimacy and shared time.

His most recent film, “Amílcar” premiered at IDFA, where it received the Outstanding Artistic Contribution Award in the Envision Competition.

He delved further into the making of his film with Variety:

You describe the act of making music as something almost mysterious. Did spending time with these musicians change the way you understand your own creative process as a filmmaker?

It was, in many ways, a journey of discovery. I wanted to explore the mystery of creation through music, which I have always considered perhaps the most mysterious of all art forms.

What I discovered, particularly through the time I spent with these musicians, was how many similarities there are between their creative processes and mine. Listening, for instance, is the first step towards creation. Joana, Emil and Vasco devote a great deal of time to inhabiting places, observing and listening to their surroundings, allowing landscapes and the people who inhabit them to offer clues about the music that will eventually emerge.

This made me realize that creation does not necessarily originate within ourselves. It also comes from what surrounds us, from our capacity to pay attention and to remain receptive to the world. I found many more parallels with my own experience of documentary filmmaking than I had anticipated.

All three musicians work outside the mainstream music industry, working with both inherited traditions and contemporary tools. Do you see their independence as an artistic choice, a necessity, or a way of resisting the increasingly standardized nature of the music business?

From the beginning, I wanted to explore forms of creation beyond the pressures of the music industry. I find it difficult to imagine these musicians preserving their freedom in terms of time, experimentation and working methods within increasingly standardized structures. Their independence is not simply an act of resistance; it allows a different approach to creation, rooted in craftsmanship, patience and a close relationship with their surroundings. For me, this is both a political and artistic choice: protecting the conditions in which something genuinely unexpected can emerge.

How do you balance observational intimacy and trust with the inevitable influence of the camera and filmmaking team on the creative process?

In ‘Dryads,’ I return to a working method developed in previous films, beginning with a pact of trust with the people I film. I then maintain a relatively static, unobtrusive presence. Over time, life and the creative process take over, and our small crew becomes part of the landscape. We never disappear completely, but we stop being a source of disturbance.

I don’t believe complete observational distance exists, nor should it be the goal. What matters is building a relationship in which the camera does not fundamentally alter the process being filmed. That is when a certain authenticity becomes possible, and the material that ultimately matters in the editing room begins to emerge.

The landscapes in ‘Dryads’ seem to become active participants in the creative process. Were you interested in exploring the idea that music is not simply created by individuals, but also emerges from a dialogue with place, memory and nature?

Absolutely. This is one of the central ideas of the film. We live in a time dominated by noise, haste, the constant distractions of our screens and a certain dehumanization of our relationship with the world. Through Emil, Vasco and Joana, I wanted to explore a less anthropocentric perspective, one grounded in listening and in a humbler relationship with our surroundings.

Nature and chance contribute something essential to the creative process that lies beyond our control and even beyond our understanding. The landscape is not simply a backdrop or a source of inspiration; it becomes an active presence, almost another collaborator. It can suggest, interrupt, transform and redirect the music. I find something reassuring in accepting that creation is not entirely under our control. Perhaps learning to surrender part of that control is precisely what allows something new to happen. Chance and uncertainty are essential to my work, as they are for many filmmakers who embrace nonfiction.

The 17th year DOC NYC Manhattan runs Nov. 11-19 and continues online through Nov. 29.

#696. A grant to hand out more grants — and build a research area

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Virginia Gewin is a freelance reporter in Portland, Oregon.

Grants worth up to US$10,000 will fund niche scientific problems.Credit: SimpleImages/Getty

Amid political instability and decreased funding for science worldwide, some non-profit organizations are testing whether and how microgrants — awards of US$10,000 or less — can spur innovation. The latest development comes from the Experiment Foundation, a non-profit science funding organization in Berkeley, California, which has launched the Field Building Accelerator to cultivate ingenuity hubs around specific fields of research using small, rapidly deployed grants.

The initiative will, in early 2027, award at least 50 individuals — called field builders — $70,000 each. The recipients, in turn, will design their own microgrant programme to distribute up to $10,000 to researchers exploring distinct facets of the same niche scientific problem. The grants will be hosted on Experiment.com, an online platform that allows organizations to advertise and fund research projects.

“We want to create a different persona in science — the people who can chart new research territory,” says David Lang, executive director of the Experiment Foundation.

The accelerator programme is open to proposals that broadly target oceans, climate, toxicity, future science and conservation technology, says Lang — reflecting the interests of its funders, including non-profit organizations such as the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation in Palo Alto, California. Prospective field builders must propose a name for the field, define its core questions and challenges, and identify at least eight researchers, laboratories or communities they would consider funding.

Judges will select field builders who they think are best placed to identify overlooked talent, back unproven ideas and bring like-minded researchers together. Ideally, says Lang, they will reflect diverse scientific perspectives, including early-career researchers, science journalists, science-fiction authors and venture capitalists. “There are people that build momentum in scientific fields, but they are different from the ones who are getting big publications or spinning out companies,” he says.

And, in a bid to take chances on unconventional ideas, the judges will not average scores; instead, if any of the two or three judges champions an application, it moves forward.

Although some might baulk at the idea that $10,000 grants are large enough to spur new research disciplines, others say it is time to experiment with new ways to distribute research funding. “If we really want to help to seed challenging, high risk, ‘who knows what will happen’ ideas, then small-scale grants are a good strategy,” says Brian Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science, a non-profit organization in Charlottesville, Virginia, that promotes transparent and reproducible science.

In 2025, The Science Foundation in Seattle, Washington, organized public donations to award up to $10,000 to researchers who have a compelling ‘what if’ basic-science proposal in the areas of mathematics, physical sciences and biological sciences. The foundation announced the second round of winners on 12 November.

#695. Wael Mohya could make German football history at 17

At just 17, Gladbach forward Wael Mohya has earned his first Germany call-up. The dual-national talent has chosen the DFB path for now — and could soon make modern national-team history.

If you watch the Bundesliga, then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer. But not even the 17-year-old (Mohya turns 18 on December 31) Borussia Mönchengladbach youngster would have expected to be called up to the Germany squad so soon.

"Of course, I was absolutely thrilled. It means a great, great deal to me. I think everyone dreams of being selected for the national team at some point," Mohya said.

"And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud."

Mohya was at the gym when the call came in. He then shared the good news with his parents over dinner. "They started crying," the teenager said in a video posted on Gladbach's social media channels.

The youngster, who was born in a small town east of Düsseldorf, smiles and laughs a lot in interviews. He is always friendly, and in a good mood. On the field, too, he exudes the lightheartedness and carefree spirit of a 17-year-old.

As a technically skilled and creative player, Mohya often seeks out one-on-one situations and puts his opponents under pressure with quick dribbles. In nine Bundesliga appearances this season, Mohya has scored twice and delivered one assist.

"He's so cool and just plays really well. It's fun to watch him," Borussia coach Alexander Blessin said recently.

"Wael brings a lot to the team with his laid-back attitude on the field. He's not afraid to take risks, no matter how much pressure there is," added Gladbach's sporting director Rouven Schröder at a talk show on Sport1.

Borussia Mönchengladbach has been Mohya's sporting home since he was seven years old. Last season, previous head coach Eugen Polanski promoted him to the first team, and in December 2025, Mohya made his Bundesliga debut. Against Wolfsburg, aged 16 years and 347 days old, he became the youngest Bundesliga player in the club's history.

Mohya also recently completed a voluntary social year at an elementary school in Mönchengladbach. This is a program in Germany for young people who volunteer in the social sector — at hospitals, schools, or nursing homes, for example — for about six to 18 months. They gain work experience, help others, and earn a little money.

At the school's open all-day care program, Mohya helped serve meals, assisted children with their homework, and played with them. That's also where his nickname comes from. Because a girl hadn't understood his first name correctly or couldn't pronounce it, she called him "Waffel." Now, that name has stuck.

Even before being called up to the Germany team, clubs in the Bundesliga and across Europe's top leagues had taken notice of Mohya and were trying to sign him. His contract with Borussia Mönchengladbach runs through 2028.

With Gladbach currently in a relegation battle, his future appears likely to be elsewhere. If the club wants to generate transfer revenue from its biggest talent, next summer would likely be the opportunity to sell him — unless he extends his contract with Borussia.

The 17-year-old's career is managed by his parents. Whichever club can convince them that their son is in good hands and help him reach his full potential likely has the best chance of securing Mohya's signing.

Mohya himself says he doesn't even know how much he's currently earning at Gladbach.

"My parents take care of all that," he told Bild recently. "I get a monthly allowance, which is more than enough for me."

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp recently revealed how much he had enjoyed his conversations with the youngster.

"The conversations I had with him were great," Klopp said with a laugh. "I wasn't that confident at 17, but then again, I wasn't that good either."

Since Mohya's parents are from Morocco, their son also holds Moroccan citizenship. As a result, he could have played for Morocco, but he has now decided against it. In fact, the Moroccan football association had been actively courting Mohya as early as last year and had already reached out to him in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.

Now, like Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib, Mohya will continue to play in the German jersey, unlike Schalke's Soufiane El-Faouzi, who chose Morocco, or Bayer Leverkusen's Ibrahim Maza, who likely would have been selected by Klopp as well if he hadn't already opted for Algeria.

For Mohya, who played for Germany's youth teams from the U16s through to the U21s, the door to Morocco remains open, even if he does play for Germany. According to FIFA regulations, players under the age of 21 can change national teams before their fourth international match (whether a competitive or friendly match), provided that none of those matches take place during a World Cup or a continental tournament such as the European Championship, Copa America, or Africa Cup of Nations.

If Mohya plays in the upcoming UEFA Nations League games in Serbia or against the Netherlands, another record is on the horizon. Although there were two even younger players who made their debuts in the Germany jersey — Willy Baumgärtner in 1908 (at 17 years and 104 days) and Marius Hiller in 1910 (at 17 years and 241 days) — the era in which they debuted is hardly comparable. And so, while Wael Mohya would rank third overall on the list, he would become the youngest Germany player in the modern era. The youngest to date was Hamburg legend Uwe Seeler in 1954, aged 17 years and 345 days.

Sufferin' succotash! The Monstars and Tune Squad interplanetary slam arrived 30 years ago, and it's still a clinic in interplanetary conflict resolution.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

While "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”

It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

"Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max.
